docs.text: The cui-proxy operator guide

docs.title: Real systems. Less exposure.
docs.text:
A local, fail-closed proxy for Codex CLI that replaces sensitive data with synthetic values before it reaches the model and restores the originals in streamed responses, so your coding agent's tool calls still run against real systems.

Get started Follow a request

docs.title: What the proxy does
docs.text:
Codex sends supported model requests to a loopback listener on your machine. With the default sanitize policy, matching values become synthetic stand-ins: an address becomes a documentation-range address, a dictionary hostname becomes an .example name, and an opaque token becomes a REDACTED-… value. A local vault remembers the mapping. Supported streamed response text and tool arguments are restored before Codex uses them.

With strict, a detected value stops the entire request. You can also mask most values while blocking selected rules. Neither policy improves what the detectors can recognize; your dictionaries and regex rules extend their coverage.

Component Job Default location Codex Sends requests and executes approved local tools Your client Proxy Inspects, masks or blocks; restores streamed responses Loopback port 8787 Dashboard Shows activity/configuration and tests text locally Loopback port 8788 YAML and dictionaries Define your policy and sensitive-name coverage ~/.config/cui-proxy/ Vault Stores real ↔ synthetic mappings Memory by default; optional encrypted file Decision log Records decisions and rule counts without request content ~/.local/state/cui-proxy/decisions.jsonl

Understand the boundary

Detection is pattern- and dictionary-based. Unmatched content can leave the machine. Credentials pass through, some protocol fields have inspection exceptions, and unsupported payloads are refused. This is not a DLP product or a compliance approval. Read capabilities and limitations before using it with sensitive material; CUI use still requires the relevant GOVSEC / ISSM approval.

docs.title: How cui-proxy handles a request
docs.text:
cui-proxy sits between a configured Codex client and its model backend. It replaces detected values before forwarding supported requests, keeps a local mapping, and restores known replacements in supported response fields. It is a pattern-based exposure reduction tool, not a complete data classifier or a compliance guarantee.

Start with the quick start, follow the tutorial, or use Codex setup to connect a client.

docs.title: Where the proxy sits
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Codex client] -->|Model request| P[cui-proxy on localhost]
    P -->|Inspected request| U[Configured model backend]
    U -->|SSE response| P
    P -->|Restored response| C
    C -->|Separate execution permission| T[Local tools: shell, Git, SSH]
    T -->|Tool output enters later model requests| C

Only traffic routed through the proxy is inspected. Git, SSH, shell commands, and their network connections do not run through this HTTP proxy. A command, remote URL, or tool result can nevertheless be detected when Codex sends it to the model on a later turn. Command approval and SSH authentication are separate from proxy policy.

The proxy API and dashboard use separate localhost listeners, conventionally ports 8787 and 8788. The native-client guard rejects browser Origin and Fetch Metadata requests; in loopback mode it also checks Host to resist DNS rebinding. Non-loopback binding requires an explicit setting and does not add authentication or TLS. Other native processes running as the same OS user are inside the local trust boundary.

docs.title: The request lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Receive native client request] --> B[Route, encoding and metadata guards]
    B --> C[Read bounded request body]
    C --> D[Codex adapter: parse supported JSON]
    D --> A1[Opt-in attachments: replace with local extracted text]
    A1 --> E[Detectors find spans; merge overlaps]
    A1 -->|Extraction fails or attachment unsupported| X
    E --> F{Any blocking match?}
    F -->|Yes| X[Record blocked decision and reject]
    F -->|No| G[Vault supplies synthetics; verify restoration]
    G --> H[Record forwarding decision]
    H --> I[Forward to configured upstream]
    I --> J[Validate response framing and encoding]
    J --> K[Restore supported SSE fields]
    K --> L[Return restored stream to client]
    B -->|Guard fails| X
    D -->|Unsupported or invalid| X
  1. Take the active configuration snapshot. A request uses a consistent policy, sanitizer, and restorer. Rule reloads affect later requests.
  2. Apply guards. The adapter accepts POST /v1/responses and GET /v1/models; it strips /v1 for the upstream route. Unknown routes, compressed request bodies, unsuitable native-client headers, and detected values in fields that cannot be rewritten are refused. Model listings are a body-free passthrough route, with the request guards still applied.
  3. Inspect metadata. The Codex adapter decodes X-Codex-Turn-Metadata and sanitizes workspaces and cwd, including workspace map keys and remote URLs. Other metadata fields are inspected without rewriting. Malformed, repeated, oversized, or over-deep metadata fails closed. The fixed metadata limit is 64 KiB.
  4. Parse the body. The Responses request must be a single valid UTF-8 JSON object, within the configured body limit (20 MiB by default) and fixed nesting limit of 64 containers. Attachments default to block. With the extraction setting, supported inline PDFs and PNG/JPEG images become local text before detection; filenames and binary bytes are dropped. File references, audio and other unsupported forms block. Extraction limits and failures always block, including under passthrough.
  5. Detect and decide. All configured detectors run on supported values. Overlaps become a union so a shorter match cannot leave part of another detected value exposed. Any effective blocking match rejects the request before forwarding; otherwise the sanitizer replaces the detected spans.
  6. Allocate mappings and check restoration. The vault reserves detected originals, avoids collisions, and supplies stable synthetics. The sanitizer checks that the restorer can find exactly the inserted replacements. A bounded replacement that fails that check is retried as an opaque secret token; a failed retry blocks by default.
  7. Record the decision and forward. The decision log is written before forwarding. It records metadata such as request ID, outcome, rule names, and counts, without request text or original values. With strict policy, a failed audit write prevents forwarding. Sanitize defaults to warning and continuing on an audit failure; set audit.on_error: block to require it.
  8. Restore the supported stream. The response adapter recognizes SSE events, restores known synthetics in supported fields, and sends the result back with Cache-Control: no-store.

docs.title: What is inspected and what stays unchanged
docs.text:
Location Behavior Prompt text, instructions, tool descriptions and results, schema strings, ordinary string leaves Detect and sanitize, or block according to effective action Non-protocol object keys Inspected too: sensitive values can be used as map keys Strings containing valid JSON objects or arrays Parse recursively and inspect decoded keys and leaves, including escaped text Integer literals Inspect; a sanitized integer becomes a JSON string Decimal and exponent numbers Check original and exact expanded digits; detected values are refused to avoid a lossy rewrite; exponents outside ±400 are refused Known protocol identifiers such as model, role, tool names and IDs at their protocol positions Preserve; when any rule blocks, check against blocking rules without rewriting Known include values Preserve as protocol entries; unknown entries are inspected Vendor encrypted_content in reasoning/compaction items Preserve unscanned; with any blocking rule, require base64/base64url-shaped content Workspace cwd and workspaces metadata Sanitize or block using the body rules and vault Remaining metadata, non-credential headers and query string Inspect; any detection blocks because these fields are not safely rewritten Authorization, Cookie, Chatgpt-Account-Id headers Forward as credentials, unscanned and unchanged

Nested JSON is inspected as data, not by running a regex over serialized escape syntax. Matches that cross JSON structural tokens cannot be safely rewritten and are refused. A string merely named id in arbitrary tool data does not automatically receive the protocol exemption.

Encrypted reasoning remains a boundary: a value written entirely in the accepted ciphertext alphabet could pass there. Credential passthrough is also intentional; the proxy must retain the credentials needed by the upstream.

docs.title: The vault and response restoration
docs.text:
The vault holds both directions of each mapping: original to synthetic and synthetic to original. Derivation uses a keyed HMAC and the replacement class; collision checks keep synthetics distinct from known originals and existing mappings. Reusing the same mapping lets Codex resend conversation history without repeatedly masking an issued synthetic. An ambiguous address from the IPv4 overflow pool is treated more cautiously and can block.

Vault mode Operational consequence memory Mappings disappear on restart; an old conversation's synthetics may no longer restore file Mappings are persisted encrypted with AES-256-GCM and a local key file; protect both files and preserve them together

File mode saves changed mappings periodically (every 30 seconds by default) and on graceful shutdown. An abrupt process or machine failure can lose changes since the last successful save; it is not a per-request durable transaction.

The vault contains originals and is sensitive even though the decision log does not contain them. The configuration guide explains file paths and restart requirements; rules explains the available shapes.

Supported streamed deltas include output text, refusals, reasoning summaries, function-call arguments, and custom tool input. The restorer buffers incomplete synthetic prefixes across chunks. Function-call arguments are handled as JSON, so restored quotes, backslashes, escaped text, keys, and numeric values retain valid structure. They have a fixed 20 MiB cumulative argument-delta input limit per response and a 20 MiB completed argument-document limit. Invalid or unfinished argument JSON cuts the stream.

Restoration is field-aware. Protocol identifiers, opaque blobs, unknown delta event types, and non-summary reasoning content are not broadly rewritten. The model must return a known synthetic in a supported field for restoration to occur; paraphrased or modified replacements are not guaranteed to restore.

Successful model responses must be unencoded SSE. Unlabelled SSE can be recognized using a bounded framing probe; unrecognized successful bodies fail closed with stream_rewrite. Ordinary upstream error responses and model listings preserve their status and body. Redirects other than 304 are refused, so a client cannot follow a redirected request outside the configured route.

docs.title: Decisions, errors, and practical limits
docs.text:
A policy match is a decision, not a sanitizer error. A blocking rule cannot be overridden by policy.on_error. Unsupported content also always blocks. The optional policy.on_error: passthrough setting applies only to eligible sanitizer failures and can forward the original body; it is invalid with strict policy or any explicit blocking rule. Keep the default block unless you have deliberately accepted that exposure.

The decision log records the decision made before forwarding, not proof of successful model completion. A later upstream or stream failure can follow a recorded forwarding decision. See the decision log and troubleshooting for interpretation.

Patterns can miss sensitive content. The built-in bundle does not discover every hostname, username, path, or organization identifier. Add relevant dictionary and regex rules, test with fabricated values, and review limitations before depending on a policy.

Continue with rule mechanics, policy profiles, testing, the dashboard, or the complete reference. The glossary explains the terminology.

docs.title: Intended use and trust boundary
docs.text:
cui-proxy is a local inspection and reversible masking layer for supported Codex text requests and HTTP/SSE responses. It reduces accidental disclosure of values its configured rules recognize. Use it on a trusted, single-user workstation for workflows that are already authorized to use the selected upstream. Each environment supplies its own private configuration and literal dictionaries outside this source repository.

The native client, operating-system account, configuration, vault key, and configured upstream are trusted. Browser requests and DNS-rebound Host names are refused by the proxy API. This is not authentication against another native process running as the same user. Do not expose the listener as a shared network service without separate authentication, TLS, and resource controls; allow_non_loopback does not provide those controls.

docs.text:
Failure Protection and regression evidence Sensitive numbers forwarded in decimal/exponent form; short custom numeric IDs ignored Every number is checked; sensitive decimal/exponent forms fail closed; internal/adapter/codex/numeric_test.go Quadratic IPv6 candidate scanning on long punctuation input Bound parsing work to representable address suffixes; internal/detect/cost_test.go Unsupported successful model responses bypass restoration Require recognized, unencoded SSE; otherwise HTTP 502; internal/proxy/response_guard_test.go Browser/rebinding requests reach the restoration vault Native-client and loopback Host checks; persisted block decisions; internal/proxy/client_guard_test.go Extra YAML documents silently ignored; invalid ports accepted Single-document parsing and port validation; internal/config/hardening_test.go Large retention values overflow and delete fresh audit history Bound retention to 0–106751 days at configuration and log API boundaries; internal/decisionlog/hardening_test.go Parser errors expose configuration values through service logs/reload responses Service-facing errors suppress values; explicit check-config retains diagnostics; CLI regression tests Concurrent processes overwrite a shared file vault Hold an exclusive vault lock from load through final save; cmd/cui-proxy/vault_lock_test.go

The minimum toolchain is Go 1.26.11. An initial govulncheck scan of Go 1.26.0 reported standard-library vulnerabilities; a scan using the patched toolchain reported none. For example, the Go advisory for GO-2026-6809 identifies 1.26.10 as fixed. Go 1.26.11 additionally fixes GO-2026-6859. CI and release jobs run make vuln against the current advisory database; a clean scan is time-specific evidence, not a guarantee of absence of bugs.

docs.title: Workspace metadata
docs.text: From v0.3.2, Codex workspaces and cwd header fields use the request sanitizer and vault (including workspace keys and Git remote URLs). Other metadata fields are inspected after decoding and remain unchanged. Strict or explicit block rules still reject detections. Invalid metadata fails closed even under passthrough. Regression and fuzz coverage lives in internal/adapter/codex/metadata_test.go and internal/proxy/metadata_test.go; verification records the synthetic live probe. Credentials remain an inspection exception.

docs.title: Optional local attachment processing
docs.text: The attachment mode requires maintained Poppler and Tesseract installations. Native parsers run as the proxy user with capped input/output, time and concurrency; they are not isolated by an OS sandbox or hard memory limit. They receive no inherited credentials and perform no remote fetches. Only extracted text enters the sanitizer and upstream request. OCR recognition can be incomplete or incorrect; detector coverage remains limited.

docs.title: Deployment and routine checks
docs.text:
1. Build with the required patched Go toolchain. Run make test, make lint, make fuzz, and make vuln before distributing a modified binary.
  2. Keep configuration, dictionaries, vault/key files and audit storage in a private directory. Avoid sensitive identifiers in rule names: names are deliberately retained in diagnostics and decision records.
  3. Run cui-proxy check-config -config /private/path/config.yaml and cui-proxy policy check -config /private/path/config.yaml. For a custom compiled adapter, use the same -adapter with check-config and serve.
  4. Use policy.on_error: block. Set audit.on_error: block when delivery must stop if recording fails; sanitize mode otherwise defaults to warn. Choose strict when detected values must be refused instead of masked.
  5. Run test-rules with fabricated samples covering your own rules, then repeat the live smoke when changing clients or upstreams.
  6. Validate edits before reloading. A failed reload retains the current policy; startup/reload log errors direct you to explicit validation. Restart-only settings require a restart, as documented in the README.
  7. Verify audit chains regularly with audit verify, and monitor disk space, blocked requests, errors, audit-write failures, and vault-save warnings.

docs.title: Demonstrated scope and remaining limits
docs.text:
The live evidence records ChatGPT-authenticated Codex CLI 0.167.0 with gpt-6-astra, exact IP/OCID restoration, and a shell tool round trip using fabricated data. Local tests cover policy blocks, error handling, reloads, framing, concurrency and storage. These checks do not establish detection accuracy for arbitrary customer data.

  • Patterns and dictionaries can miss information, including semantic meaning, unfamiliar encodings, names and local paths absent from configured rules. strict blocks detections; it cannot classify every restricted fact.
  • Credential headers and vendor encrypted reasoning content are documented inspection exceptions. A malicious client can bypass the proxy entirely.
  • Restoration does not validate a model's reasoning or make generated commands safe. Keep Codex tool permissions and normal human review in place.
  • Memory-mode restarts lose mappings. File mode checkpoints every 30 seconds and on graceful shutdown; abrupt termination or storage failure can lose recent mappings. Preserve the key and vault together, and begin a fresh client conversation after losing state.
  • Vault growth and aggregate concurrency are not globally bounded. Per-request limits and bounded parsing do not replace OS resource controls.
  • Audit chains are tamper-evident, not externally anchored. A writer who owns the files can rewrite an entire chain or remove its newest tail.
  • Long-session compaction, websocket transport and arbitrary future response event types are outside the recorded live smoke. Unknown request routes are refused. Stream restoration covers output text, refusals, reasoning summaries, function-call arguments and custom-tool input deltas. Unknown delta events, non-summary reasoning events and non-JSON event data pass through unchanged. Other JSON events restore eligible string fields while preserving opaque fields; this does not guarantee future event compatibility.

This review supports use as an additional local safeguard within those boundaries. It is not a compliance certification or permission to transmit restricted data. Organizational approvals, approved-account enforcement and network controls remain separate responsibilities; deferred approval formats must not be represented as implemented controls.

docs.title: Local attachment inspection
docs.text:
Available from v0.4.0

Upgrade to v0.4.0 or newer and restart the running proxy before enabling policy.attachments. The v0.3.3 release does not accept this setting. Re-run cui-proxy menubar install after upgrading to refresh the app and its bundled offline manual.

Attachments are blocked by default. To replace supported attachments with locally extracted, sanitized text, merge the following partial edit into the existing policy section of your YAML. Keep the rest of your configuration, validate it with check-config, and reload (or restart) the proxy:

policy:
  attachments: extract_text # block is the default
  on_error: block
  max_body_bytes: 20971520  # includes base64 overhead for the whole request

cui-proxy policy check -config PATH and the dashboard show the attachment mode. The setting uses the same per-request snapshot as your detector rules. Changing it does not change requests already being processed. Existing binaries must be rebuilt/upgraded before this setting is accepted.

For a complete starting configuration, download attachment-text.yaml and its fabricated hosts.txt dictionary. Follow the recipe setup to validate and select the file.

docs.title: What reaches the model
docs.text:
Supported attachments are replaced by input_text parts before the existing sanitizer runs. Only extracted text reaches the model. Original bytes, filenames, image details and file metadata are discarded. The sanitize profile masks rule matches; strict and action: block rules refuse matches in extracted text. Conversion mode blocks all body-processing failures, even if policy.on_error: passthrough was configured, so a later sanitizer failure cannot send the original attachment. Unsupported shapes always block in either mode.

This is text extraction, not document redaction or a complete visual inspection. Layout, diagrams, handwriting and unreadable text may be lost. PDF pages with a text layer use that layer; embedded images on those pages are not OCRed. OCR uses English and may misrecognize sensitive text, affecting detection. Review the applicability of your rules to extracted text. This mode cannot provide the model with the original image or document layout.

docs.title: Supported input and local tools
docs.text:
Direct content parts of unambiguous Responses API user messages support:

  • input_file with file_data: "data:application/pdf;base64,..." and optional string filename.
  • input_image with image_url: "data:image/png;base64,..." or "data:image/jpeg;base64,..." and optional detail: auto|low|high.

Images in function and custom tool results are also converted when they are direct parts of an array-valued output in a top-level input item of type function_call_output or custom_tool_call_output. The item must have a nonempty string call_id and no duplicate fields. The same input_image formats and detail values listed above apply. Each image becomes an input_text part; surrounding text, output order and call identity are preserved. Extracted tool text follows the same sanitization and blocking rules as user attachments. All attachments share the request's extraction budgets. This supports tools returning screenshots without forwarding the screenshots themselves.

Tool-result PDFs, computer-use output items, images nested in arbitrary objects, and attachments in assistant messages remain unsupported. Objects encoded inside text are inspected as text/embedded JSON and do not acquire attachment conversion privileges. Tool names do not affect eligibility. This is a protocol-position allowlist, not a restriction to particular tools.

Uploaded file_id references, remote URLs, audio, other MIME types, bare base64, duplicate or unknown fields, and attachments in other positions are refused. There are no remote downloads or cloud OCR calls.

Install maintained Poppler tools (pdfinfo, pdftotext, pdftoppm) for PDFs and Tesseract with English language data for images and PDF pages without text. Executables must be on the proxy process's PATH, which may differ from a terminal's PATH when launched from a menu bar or service. For example, Homebrew on macOS provides brew install poppler tesseract. Restart the proxy after changing its tool environment. Tesseract's command-line documentation describes its local stdin/stdout OCR interface.

A PDF page with no text is rendered locally and OCRed. Every page must yield text; blank or unreadable pages, encrypted PDFs, missing tools and failed extraction block the request. Tools run without a shell or inherited credentials; stderr is discarded. PDF bytes are temporarily stored in a private directory (file mode 0600), removed on normal completion or cancellation. Abrupt process termination may leave a temporary directory. The tools run as the proxy user, not inside an OS security sandbox; use maintained installations.

docs.title: Limits and diagnostics
docs.text:
Per request: eight attachments, 10 MiB total decoded input, twenty total PDF pages, 2 MiB extracted text and thirty seconds including time waiting for an extraction slot. Input images are limited to sixteen million pixels. PDF raster pages are scaled to at most 4000 pixels on their longest side. Two tool processes run concurrently across requests, with capped output and cancellation. These limits do not impose a hard OS memory limit on the external parsers. The normal request-body size limit also applies before conversion.

Attachment refusals retain 422 reason=sanitize kind=bad_body, with a safe detail code and a fixed explanation, for example:

detail=attachment_pdf_missing_tool. A local extraction tool is missing. Install Poppler ...

Categories are pdf, image, file, audio or binary. The cause explains the next step:

Cause Meaning Action disabled Attachment processing is off Enable extract_text only for the supported inline formats, or paste text reference A URL or uploaded file ID cannot be inspected locally Send inline data or paste text; the proxy does not fetch it unsupported Unsupported format or encrypted PDF Export an unlocked PDF or PNG/JPEG image, or paste text shape Duplicate, unknown or misplaced attachment fields or tool envelope Use a supported user-message content part or direct function/custom tool-result image invalid Invalid encoding, image or document Re-export a valid document/image limit A count, size, page, pixel or text limit was exceeded Split or reduce the input missing_tool Local extractor executable is unavailable Install Poppler/Tesseract and check the service PATH failed An extractor returned failure Check tool/language-data installation or re-export the document empty A page or image yielded no readable text Supply clearer input or paste text timeout Processing exceeded the time budget or was cancelled Reduce/split the input and retry The code appears in the response, server log and hash-chained decision log; cui-proxy explain REQUEST-ID displays the remedy. No filenames, URLs, extracted contents or tool error text are logged. Existing records retain their original hashes; older proxy binaries cannot verify new records carrying the detail field. Historical records without details cannot recover an attachment's exact failure cause.

If a client retries the same rejected image history, retrying alone cannot repair its placement or encoding. Use text output or begin a fresh session without the unsupported result. Do not disable blocking rules or enable passthrough to recover. Install the updated proxy binary and restart the running service to use tool-result image extraction; reloading configuration alone cannot add support to an older binary.

docs.title: Check the running service before attachment work
docs.text:
Run cui-proxy preflight -config PATH after starting the service, or use Check readiness in the dashboard. The dashboard checks once on initial load. This queries the running dashboard's guarded /api/preflight endpoint; it does not substitute dependency discovery from the terminal's environment.

The versioned JSON report identifies the running process (version, Go version, build revision when available and PID), effective policy enums, and dependency checks. With attachments: extract_text, it discovers pdfinfo, pdftotext, pdftoppm and tesseract through the service PATH, then checks eng through tesseract --list-langs using the same restricted child environment as extraction. Each tool result has a fixed remedy. Tool paths, stderr, language list contents and credentials are never returned.

Install Poppler for PDF tools and Tesseract with English data for OCR. Ensure the service PATH finds them and restart the service after installation or service-environment changes. Extraction does not inherit TESSDATA_PREFIX or other shell variables, so English data must be available through the tool's default data discovery. A successful check confirms discovery and language listing, not that every document will extract successfully.

Probes have a two-second deadline, 64 KiB output cap, one concurrent probe per checker and the existing extraction slot bound. Dependency results are cached for ten seconds; policy is read fresh each time. Wait ten seconds to recheck a repaired dependency. With attachments blocked, no extraction tools are required or probed; readiness means ready for that effective policy, not OCR capability.

The CLI returns exit 0 for ready, 1 for unavailable/not-ready service or incompatible report, and 2 for usage errors. It accepts only a loopback HTTP service and never follows redirects. It prints the running build identity; dev or an unavailable revision cannot establish an exact binary revision. Keep detailed CLI output captured locally as described in verification guidance.

docs.title: Block diagnostics
docs.text:
A blocked request is answered with an OpenAI-style JSON error whose code is the block reason (route, body_too_large, compressed, header, policy, sanitize, unrestorable, bad_request, client, audit, internal; audit is HTTP 503 and means the decision log could not be written, see Decision log). When the body or structured metadata could not be sanitized, the message also names a kind and, when one span caused it, the detector rule (a name from your config, never a value):

cui-proxy: request blocked (reason=sanitize kind=pool_exhausted rule=builtin.ipv4)

Every error also carries a request_id= you can give to cui-proxy explain. The same appears in the proxy log as request blocked (reason=... kind=... rule=... class=...), and in the dashboard feed as sanitize:<kind> or header:<kind> with a blocked:<rule> count. The metrics count blocks by reason only.

kind meaning what to do pool_exhausted no synthetic left for the class (see Synthetic address pool) plan a fresh vault only after ending affected conversations; old synthetics cannot be restored without their mappings. Preserve the existing file/key pair before switching to new file paths, or restart memory mode ambiguous a value equals an issued overflow synthetic (or a zero-padded spelling of one) see Synthetic address pool pseudonym no synthetic can be made for the value (e.g. an invalid CIDR from a custom rule) fix the rule's pattern or synth class rule_match a blocking rule matched (code policy for the body, header for metadata: strict profile or action: block) expected: remove the value, or use the sanitize profile / a rule without action: block if masking is allowed unrestorable the sanitized text would not restore even after downgrading (code unrestorable) rare: report the rule and kind from the log line bad_body invalid JSON/UTF-8 or unsupported content; for metadata also invalid shape, repeated headers, over 64 KiB, or a match in an unchanged field check the request shape and reported rule using fabricated input depth JSON nested deeper than 64 levels expected for pathological input other any other failure check the log line

A value whose synthetic would not restore where it stands (for example id:fe80::1, ID123-45-6789 or x4111 1111 1111 1111, where the address/number synthetic would be glued to a letter or hex digit) is not blocked: it is masked as a REDACTED-<8hex> token instead and counted as downgraded in the metrics.

For Git/SSH failures, first identify whether the error comes from the model request or the local command. See the configuration walkthrough for the decision table and supported overrides.

docs.title: Attachment-specific details
docs.text:
Attachments default to policy.attachments: block. With policy.attachments: extract_text, supported inline PDFs and PNG/JPEG images are converted locally, then sanitized; original attachment bytes are never forwarded. See Attachment inspection for tools and limits.

Attachment errors retain reason=sanitize kind=bad_body and add a safe detail=attachment_<category>_<cause> plus a fixed remedy. For example, attachment_file_disabled identifies the default refusal; attachment_file_reference identifies a file ID or URL that cannot be inspected; attachment_pdf_missing_tool identifies missing local extraction software. shape, unsupported, invalid, limit, failed, empty, and timeout distinguish other failures. Details are persisted for cui-proxy explain without filenames or contents. Old records without details cannot recover the cause.

docs.title: Recovery metadata and repeated refusals
docs.text:
Proxy-generated JSON errors retain their existing HTTP status, error.code, error.type, message and request ID. They additionally include error.recovery with a closed code, category, retry, and fixed remedy text. The headers X-Cui-Proxy-Recovery-Code and X-Cui-Proxy-Retry carry the same guidance. No original values are included. Already-started streams are still aborted on restoration failure; recovery metadata cannot be added after response headers. Provider error responses retain provider semantics and are not reclassified.

Category Examples Retry action policy blocking rule, rejected metadata after_change: remove rejected content/metadata; keep protection enabled representation unsupported route, attachment shape/format, compressed input after_change: use supported input, remove the rejected representation from history dependency missing extraction tool, audit storage failure after_repair: repair the service environment or storage first budget body/depth/extraction limits, synthetic pool exhaustion, processing timeout after_change: reduce the workload; preserve mappings needed by active sessions overload extraction queue deadline (attachment_*_busy) backoff: bounded delay and lower attachment concurrency transient upstream connection failure backoff: check task state because delivery may be uncertain, then retry with a bound internal unclassified failure after_repair: investigate safe logs and request ID before retrying

For deterministic categories, category_occurrences counts that category across all clients of one handler in a one-minute window (saturating at one million). It is not proof of an identical request or a particular client's retry loop. The tracker has at most 128 entries, uses only closed diagnostic codes, expires old entries and is never persisted. It stores no bodies or content hashes. Transient/overload categories have no recurrence count. cui-proxy explain provides recovery guidance from the persisted reason/attachment detail; it does not invent recurrence counts or recover kinds absent from the decision record.

Client retry behavior is advisory: the proxy cannot force Codex or another client to honor custom headers/fields. No end-to-end suppression claim is made. If the same image or blocked value is retained in history, cancel the retrying operation, replace/remove that content locally, then start a fresh session with only permitted context if the client keeps resending it. Reopening the same session or repeating the same request is not a remedy. The proxy never deletes context or relaxes policy automatically.

docs.title: OCI and AWS CLI configuration rules
docs.text: Use these rules when CLI configuration or command output may appear in Codex prompts or tool results. They extend the existing AWS access-key rule with coverage for selected OCI configuration fields and AWS credential assignments. The proxy inspects supported model-request content; it does not watch, modify, or automatically load ~/.oci/ or ~/.aws/, or control local CLI execution.

docs.title: Know which file you are protecting
docs.text:
Source Typical contents Coverage to configure ~/.oci/config Profiles, user and tenancy OCIDs, fingerprint, key_file, region; optional pass_phrase and security_token_file Built-ins for OCIDs; custom rules below for selected assignments; dictionary for sensitive profile names and regions ~/.oci/oci_cli_rc CLI defaults, aliases, queries, compartment IDs and endpoints Built-ins for OCIDs and addresses; dictionaries for sensitive names, endpoints and other defaults OCI key and session-token files Private key material or authentication tokens Built-in private-key/JWT patterns cover recognized shapes, not every token format ~/.aws/config and ~/.aws/credentials Profiles, regions, access-key IDs, secret access keys and session tokens Separate AWS key-ID rule plus assignment rules below; dictionaries for other sensitive values

These are default paths; both CLIs support alternative locations. See Oracle's CLI configuration guide, environment-variable reference and the AWS configuration reference for their file formats and overrides.

key_file and security_token_file contain paths, not the referenced key or token. Matching those paths does not inspect their target files. Likewise, fingerprint is a public-key identifier, not a private key; mask it if your policy treats infrastructure identifiers as sensitive.

docs.title: Start with a complete recipe
docs.text:
Download cloud-cli.yaml and hosts.txt into a new private directory using the recipe download workflow. This is a complete proxy configuration, separate from either cloud CLI's configuration. It masks matches under sanitize and keeps the built-in bundle, AWS key-ID rule, service-name dictionary and tutorial ticket rule.

cloud-cli.yaml — complete configuration
# Complete configuration. Save hosts.txt beside this file.
# These rules inspect text in supported model requests, not local cloud files.
listen: localhost:8787
ui:
  listen: localhost:8788
upstreams:
  codex: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex
policy:
  profile: sanitize
  on_error: block
  unsupported: block
  max_body_bytes: 20971520
vault:
  mode: memory
audit:
  enabled: true
  file: .state/cloud-cli-decisions.jsonl
  on_error: block
rules:
  - name: builtin
    type: builtin
  - name: service-hosts
    type: dictionary
    file: hosts.txt
    synth: hostname
  - name: aws-keys
    type: regex
    pattern: '\b(?:AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b'
    synth: secret
  - name: ticket-ids
    type: regex
    pattern: '\bDEMO-[0-9]{6}\b'
    synth: secret
  # Whole INI/env assignment lines, including labels and trailing comments.
  # OCIDs and PEM private-key blocks are already in the built-in bundle.
  - name: oci-config-fields
    type: regex
    pattern: '(?im)^[ \t]*(?:export[ \t]+)?(?:fingerprint|key_file|pass_phrase|security_token_file|OCI_CLI_FINGERPRINT|OCI_CLI_KEY_FILE|OCI_CLI_PASSPHRASE|OCI_CLI_SECURITY_TOKEN_FILE)[ \t]*=[ \t]*[^\r\n]+'
    synth: secret
  - name: aws-credential-fields
    type: regex
    pattern: '(?im)^[ \t]*(?:export[ \t]+)?(?:aws_secret_access_key|aws_session_token)[ \t]*=[ \t]*[^\r\n]+'
    synth: secret

For an existing proxy config, copy only the oci-config-fields and aws-credential-fields entries into its current rules list. Retain your existing rules, especially type: builtin and aws-keys; YAML files are not merged automatically. Validate, preview and reload after editing rules. Listener or storage changes require a restart.

The two custom patterns match whole nonempty assignment lines, including the field name, optional export, spaces and value. Custom rules replace the whole match, not just a capture group. This deliberately masks entire paths and passphrases even when they contain spaces. It can also mask trailing comments. Names are case-insensitive. The patterns support INI-style entries and selected environment-variable assignments, for example:

Fabricated OCI text — not an operational config
[DEFAULT]
user=ocid1.user.oc1..demouseralpha
tenancy=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..demotenancyalpha
fingerprint=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff:aa:bb:cc:dd
key_file=/demo/.oci/demo-key.pem
pass_phrase=demo passphrase only
security_token_file=/demo/.oci/sessions/demo/token
region=us-ashburn-1

The OCIDs are masked by builtin.ocid. Fingerprint, key path, passphrase and token path assignments are masked by oci-config-fields (overlapping built-in matches may also be reported). [DEFAULT] and region=us-ashburn-1 remain unchanged unless another rule matches them.

Fabricated AWS text — not credentials
[default]
aws_access_key_id=AKIAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
aws_secret_access_key=demo-secret-only
aws_session_token=demo-session-only

The access-key ID is masked by aws-keys; the secret and session assignments are masked by aws-credential-fields. ASIA key IDs of the same length are also covered. This key-ID regex is part of the recipe and starter configuration, not the built-in bundle.

docs.title: Preview locally before enabling
docs.text:
From the directory containing the downloaded files, run these fabricated tests:

cui-proxy check-config -config cloud-cli.yaml
printf '%s\n' 'tenancy=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..demotenancyalpha' \
  'key_file=/demo/.oci/demo-key.pem' \
  'export OCI_CLI_PASSPHRASE=demo-passphrase-only' \
  'aws_secret_access_key=demo-secret-only' \
  'AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=demo-session-only' |
  cui-proxy test-rules -config cloud-cli.yaml
printf '%s\n' 'region=us-ashburn-1' 'output=json' |
  cui-proxy test-rules -config cloud-cli.yaml

The first preview must remove the fabricated values and report the matching rules. The second stays unchanged. test-rules uses a throwaway vault, opens no listener and makes no cloud requests. It tests text matching, not a complete Codex request or response-restoration path. See testing for those checks.

If your policy requires refusal, add action: block to selected rules, or use policy.profile: strict to reject every detected value. Keep policy.on_error: block; strict also requires enabled audit with audit.on_error: block. With a blocking rule, expect matching previews to fail with exit code 1. Masking rules may restore original values in supported replies; use blocking when that behavior is unsuitable.

docs.title: Extend coverage deliberately
docs.text:
The assignment patterns do not match JSON such as {"pass_phrase":"demo"}, YAML key: value, command flags, or an assignment embedded in prose on the same line. They do not recognize an unlabeled opaque secret. A JWT or PEM block may match the built-ins, but a raw OCI security token or AWS secret is not guaranteed to have a recognizable shape. The optional export handling is text matching, not a shell parser. Test the actual representation your tools produce.

Add literal profile names, local paths, regions, endpoint hostnames, Object Storage namespaces, AWS account IDs and role ARNs to a private dictionary when your policy requires them. Use synth: secret for arbitrary names or paths. Do not put an entire INI file into a dictionary: entries are literal strings, not parsed settings. See dictionary rules.

These examples add no default protection to an existing installation. Detection remains pattern-based; unmatched text can be forwarded. The proxy does not prevent Codex from reading files or invoking cloud tools locally. Configure the client's tool permissions separately and use fabricated data for verification.

docs.title: Connect Codex
docs.text:
There are two configuration files in this setup. The proxy YAML controls inspection. Codex's TOML controls routing. A Codex -c option cannot change the proxy's policy or turn a blocking rule into a sanitizing rule.

Setting Example Meaning Proxy listen localhost:8787 Local address accepting model requests Codex provider base_url http://localhost:8787/v1 Where Codex sends those requests Proxy upstreams.codex https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex Where inspected requests go next Dashboard ui.listen localhost:8788 Browser UI; never use this as Codex's model URL

Start the proxy first. Keep the /v1 suffix in the Codex URL; the adapter maps POST /v1/responses to /responses beneath the configured upstream base. It also supports GET /v1/models. Other routes are refused.

docs.title: Try it for a single session
docs.text:
This uses your existing ChatGPT login and model selection:

codex -c 'model_provider="cui-proxy"' \
  -c 'model_providers.cui-proxy={name="cui-proxy",base_url="http://localhost:8787/v1",wire_api="responses",requires_openai_auth=true,supports_websockets=false}'

The macOS menu-bar helper also provides Copy Codex command for its configured listener. Command-line overrides apply to that invocation; they do not rewrite your TOML. To use the tutorial instance, substitute port 18787.

docs.title: Make the proxy your default
docs.text:
Back up ~/.codex/config.toml if it exists, then merge this snippet into that user-level file. With a custom CODEX_HOME, use its config.toml instead. Do not replace unrelated settings or create a second copy of an existing table.

Merge into config.toml
# Merge into your USER configuration; do not overwrite unrelated settings.
# Put this top-level key before any [table] header.
model_provider = "cui-proxy"

[model_providers.cui-proxy]
name = "cui-proxy"
base_url = "http://localhost:8787/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = true
supports_websockets = false

Download the TOML snippet.

TOML table placement matters

Put model_provider = "cui-proxy" at the top level, before any [table] header. If you put it below [model_providers.cui-proxy], it becomes a provider-table field instead of selecting your provider.

Keep any existing model setting that works with your account. Provider selection does not grant access to a model. Stop and reopen Codex after editing, then verify a fabricated request.

docs.title: Use a named Codex profile
docs.text:
If you want an explicitly selected profile, define the provider at user level and put its selection in a profile. This is a Codex profile, separate from the proxy's policy.profile.

Merge at table boundaries; keep your current top-level settings
[model_providers.cui-proxy]
name = "cui-proxy"
base_url = "http://localhost:8787/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = true
supports_websockets = false

[profiles.cui]
model_provider = "cui-proxy"

codex --profile cui

With only this profile setup, an invocation that does not select the profile can use your other default provider and bypass the proxy. Check the active route rather than assuming every Codex session is covered.

docs.title: What the provider fields mean
docs.text:
Field Why it is here name Human-readable provider label base_url Local proxy endpoint, including /v1 wire_api = "responses" Selects the protocol implemented by the adapter requires_openai_auth = true Uses OpenAI authentication for this ChatGPT-login setup supports_websockets = false Uses the HTTP/SSE transport supported by cui-proxy

These Codex fields are documented in the official configuration reference. Managed client settings may constrain provider selection. The repository's live verification names the exact client and backend tested; it does not establish compatibility with every Codex release or desktop host.

docs.title: API-key backend (separate configuration)
docs.text:
For an API-key setup, both ends must agree. In the proxy YAML, replace the existing upstream block with:

Partial proxy YAML edit
upstreams:
  codex: https://api.openai.com/v1

Restart the proxy: upstream changes are not hot-reloadable. In the Codex user TOML, use an environment-backed provider instead of the ChatGPT-login provider:

Alternative provider; do not combine authentication modes
[model_providers.cui-api]
name = "cui-proxy API"
base_url = "http://localhost:8787/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
env_key = "OPENAI_API_KEY"
requires_openai_auth = false
supports_websockets = false

[profiles.cui-api]
model_provider = "cui-api"

Supply OPENAI_API_KEY through your existing secret-management mechanism, choose a model available to that API account, then run codex --profile cui-api. Never put the key in proxy YAML, a dictionary, a screenshot, or a public issue. This is an alternate configuration based on the Responses protocol; the dated ChatGPT-login smoke test is not evidence of an API-key live test. Run your own fabricated end-to-end check before relying on it.

docs.title: Things routing does not change
docs.text:
The proxy passes credential headers to the upstream unchanged. It does not sign you in, store credentials, grant tool execution permissions, configure SSH, or intercept every network connection from your computer. Shell tools, Git, MCP servers, browser traffic, and other clients have their own network paths. Text they return to Codex is inspected when it enters a supported model request.

If the proxy is stopped, requests routed to it fail. There is no proxy-side direct fallback. To deliberately stop using the proxy, restore your previous provider selection or launch without the temporary override; that traffic will no longer be inspected by cui-proxy.

See Life of a request, Git/SSH troubleshooting, and supported overrides.

docs.title: Compatibility evidence
docs.text: See the protocol support matrix for supported fields, stream behavior, attachment limits and deterministic task-effect tests.

docs.title: Configuration walkthrough and reference
docs.text:
Checked against v0.5.0 on 2026-11-08. This guide describes implemented settings. Planned approval/account allowlists in the ADRs are not available.

Start with which file to edit, then choose a policy. For a blocked Git operation, go to Git and SSH troubleshooting.

docs.title: Which file to edit
docs.text:
File / setting Controls Does not control Proxy config.yaml, normally ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml Detection rules, masking/blocking, listeners, upstream, vault, audit SSH keys or the agent's permission to run a command Dictionary files, normally hosts.txt beside the YAML Literal sensitive names used by a type: dictionary rule An allowlist: adding a name increases detection ~/.codex/config.toml Codex's model-provider selection and URL; separate Codex settings Proxy rule actions: Codex -c cannot override the proxy YAML Git repository .git/config, SSH configuration/agent Git remote URL and SSH authentication/transport Whether model requests pass proxy inspection

cui-proxy init creates config.yaml and hosts.txt in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cui-proxy, if set, otherwise ~/.config/cui-proxy. init -dir PATH chooses another directory. It writes starter files; it does not select them for an already running service. Do not use init -force to change one setting: it overwrites both files, including your dictionary.

serve, check-config, policy check and test-rules require an explicit -config PATH. The menu-bar installer chooses the default config directory unless installed with menubar install -config PATH; Open Config Folder opens the folder for that installation. Edit the file used by the running proxy, not an unused copy in a repository. Check the dashboard's effective configuration and startup log after applying changes.

The proxy loads one YAML document. It does not merge global and project files, interpolate environment variables inside YAML, or implement --set/per-request policy overrides. Unknown YAML fields are rejected. Dictionary, vault and audit relative paths resolve against the YAML file's directory. ~ inside YAML is not expanded; use an absolute or relative path. Shell ~ in a command argument is expanded by your shell.

docs.title: First setup and a safe edit cycle
docs.text:
For a new installation only:

cui-proxy init

For an existing installation, edit its YAML directly. These commands assume the default location; substitute your actual path if it differs:

cp ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml.backup
cui-proxy version
cui-proxy check-config -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
cui-proxy policy check -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
printf '%s\n' 'git@github.com:example/demo.git host=10.20.30.15' |
  cui-proxy test-rules -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml

test-rules uses a temporary vault and tests text detection, not a complete HTTP request, header parsing, SSH connection or round trip. Use fabricated input: its output is intended for the operator and can include original unmatched text. check-config may also print detailed configuration errors.

After validation, choose Reload rules in the menu bar or dashboard for reloadable settings. Restart for the settings marked below. A reload failure leaves the old rules active. For rollback, restore the backup, validate it, and reload or restart as appropriate. Avoid running a second proxy on the same ports or file vault.

docs.title: Sanitize, strict, and overrides
docs.text:
Situation sanitize (default) strict Detected value in supported content or workspace metadata Mask it; restore eligible model-response text locally Reject the entire request Rule explicitly says action: block Reject the entire request Reject the entire request Rule explicitly says action: sanitize Mask it Invalid configuration Unsupported content, invalid metadata, unknown route Reject Reject Detection in another header/query or unchanged metadata field Reject; those fields cannot be safely rewritten Reject Audit write fails, with defaults Warn and continue Reject

sanitize means "mask what matches", not "allow everything". strict means "block detections", not "guarantee that nothing sensitive gets through". Unrecognized values are not protected by either profile.

For everyday work where masking is appropriate, edit the existing blocks:

policy:
  profile: sanitize
  on_error: block
  unsupported: block
  max_body_bytes: 20971520

Keep your current rules, upstream, vault and audit settings. Remove an explicit action: block only from rules you intend to change to masking, or set those rules to action: sanitize. Changing the profile alone does not override explicit blocking rules.

For strict operation, set policy.profile: strict, retain policy.on_error: block, remove all explicit action: sanitize entries, and ensure audit is enabled with audit.on_error: block (or omitted so the profile default applies). At least one rule is required. To make a separate starter without overwriting your live files:

cui-proxy init -dir /tmp/cui-strict-example -profile strict
cui-proxy check-config -config /tmp/cui-strict-example/config.yaml

docs.title: Flexible masking with selected hard blocks
docs.text:
This is a complete example. Save it beside a restricted-names.txt dictionary containing fabricated entries such as restricted-project before testing:

listen: 127.0.0.1:8787
ui:
  listen: 127.0.0.1:8788
upstreams:
  codex: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex
policy:
  profile: sanitize
  on_error: block
vault:
  mode: memory
audit:
  enabled: true
  on_error: block
rules:
  - name: builtin
    type: builtin
    action: sanitize
  - name: restricted-names
    type: dictionary
    file: restricted-names.txt
    synth: hostname
    action: block
  - name: aws-keys
    type: regex
    pattern: '\b(?:AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b'
    synth: secret
    action: block

Built-in matches are masked, while the two explicit rules block. A block wins if it overlaps a sanitizing rule; a later rule cannot cancel it. This example sets audit failure to block explicitly, which is stronger than the sanitize profile's default warn.

docs.title: Overrides that exist, and ones that do not
docs.text:
Want to change Supported way / limit Block a category while masking others profile: sanitize plus action: block on selected rules Change a custom match Edit its regex or dictionary and reload Stop using a rule Remove its YAML entry and reload; this stops that detection everywhere the rule applied Allow one public value while keeping the same detector No allow, exclude, exceptions list, or action: allow in v0.5.0 Disable just builtin.email No selector for individual built-in detectors. type: builtin expands to the entire bundle Override a strict detection Not supported; action: sanitize under strict is invalid Use a custom set instead of the built-in bundle Remove the bundle and supply custom rules, but this removes every built-in protection not recreated; adding a narrower regex alongside the bundle does not narrow it Different policies for different repositories Separate YAML files and proxy instances on different ports, with separate file vaults/audit logs, and explicit client routing; no automatic repository profiles Allow unsupported input or malformed metadata Not configurable; unsupported: block is the only value Approve git push / allow an SSH destination No proxy option; execution permission and Git/SSH transport are separate

There is no general "ignore this block" switch. policy.on_error: passthrough only forwards the original body for eligible sanitizer failures (such as synthetic pool exhaustion). It does not override policy matches, metadata failures, bad_body, depth/size limits, or unsupported content. It is invalid with strict or any blocking rule, and can expose original values when used. It is not a remedy for Git remote detection.

docs.title: Git and SSH troubleshooting
docs.text:
There are two paths:

flowchart LR
    C[Codex] -->|Model request| P[cui-proxy]
    P --> M[Model backend]
    C -->|Local command permission| G[git / ssh]
    G --> H[GitHub]

The proxy does not open, authorize or filter the SSH socket. It can block a model request containing a remote URL, proposed command, or earlier tool output. That can stop the agent's next turn even though SSH itself works.

What you see Where to investigate Can proxy YAML fix it? 422 reason=header ... rule=builtin.email Workspace metadata, another header, or query v0.3.2 sanitizes workspaces and cwd; strict/explicit blocks and other header matches still block 422 reason=policy kind=rule_match Active profile and named blocking rule Use masking only if appropriate, or narrow the offending custom rule; a strict exception is unavailable 422 reason=sanitize kind=bad_body Request shape/content No blanket override. Attachments (see safe text extraction), audio, invalid JSON, or other unsupported representations can trigger it; capture a synthetic reproduction Permission denied (publickey) SSH key/agent, GitHub identity and repository permissions No Connection timeout, DNS failure, connection refused Network, firewall, VPN, SSH endpoint No Codex command approval/sandbox denial The agent's execution permissions No; approve the needed action through the supported permission flow non-fast-forward or repository authorization error Git branch state or repository access No

Codex command and network approvals are separate from proxy content policy; use the narrow permission appropriate to the intended operation. See OpenAI's explanation of command and network permissions.

For git@github.com:example/demo.git, the email detector matches the git@github.com portion. In v0.3.2 with sanitize and no applicable blocking rule, supported prompt text and workspace metadata are masked rather than rejected. No SSH allowlist or disabled email detector is needed. Eligible response text is restored before the local command runs.

A separate defect in v0.3.2 and earlier can reject tool output containing JSON with an escaped newline immediately before a matched value, such as git@github.com. It reports reason=sanitize kind=bad_body, even under sanitize. The JSON escape repair in v0.3.3 fixes this in code; changing SSH permissions, disabling email detection, or enabling passthrough is not the remedy. See the dataflow regression report for the affected paths and verification scope. Upgrade to v0.3.3 or later and restart the running proxy to use the repair.

Work through these checks:

  1. Confirm cui-proxy version, then restart the running service after an upgrade. A new binary on your shell's PATH does not update an old process; the menu-bar app may also use a different binary path. Check its startup log.
  2. Run policy check with the actual service config and check the dashboard's active profile. Look for strict or explicit blocking rules.
  3. Use explain -config PATH REQUEST-ID and the proxy log's reason/kind/rule. header does not prove the workspace field was responsible; other headers and queries remain blocking. Do not post raw headers or credentials.
  4. Test the fabricated remote above with test-rules. For full metadata handling, use the workspace smoke.
  5. If the error is from Git/SSH rather than the proxy, inspect that separately. A read-only git ls-remote origin from the same repository tests remote access without pushing or changing local branches. It contacts the remote and may still need the agent's network approval. If it works in your terminal but not the agent, compare execution permissions and SSH-agent environment.

Switching an SSH remote to HTTPS is a transport choice, not a proxy policy exception. It does not fix unsupported request bodies or other sensitive content. Changing a remote is unnecessary for the v0.3.2 metadata fix.

docs.title: Defaults and all configurable fields
docs.text:
Defaults below are loader defaults, not every value in the starter file. Omitting rules does not enable built-ins automatically. init writes three entries: the built-in bundle, a dictionary, and an AWS-key regex. A sanitize config with no rules can validate but masks no detected values; strict refuses an empty rule list. The selected adapter needs an upstream; there is no default upstream in the loader.

YAML field Default Meaning / accepted values Apply listen 127.0.0.1:8787 Proxy bind address Restart ui.listen 127.0.0.1:8788 Dashboard bind address; empty uses default, not disabled Restart allow_non_loopback false Permit non-loopback bind addresses; does not add auth/TLS; menu-bar app requires loopback Restart upstreams.codex None; starter uses ChatGPT backend Absolute base URL; no embedded credentials, query or fragment; HTTPS, or HTTP loopback for testing Restart policy.profile sanitize sanitize or strict Reload policy.on_error block block or restricted, unsafe passthrough behavior above Reload policy.attachments (from v0.4.0) block block or extract_text; see Attachment inspection Reloadable; local tools required for extraction policy.unsupported block Only block accepted Fixed behavior policy.max_body_bytes 20971520 (20 MiB) Request body limit in bytes; positive integer; zero uses default, not unlimited Reload vault.mode memory memory or encrypted file Restart vault.file None Required with file mode Restart vault.key_file None Required with file mode; 32-byte key, created 0600 Restart audit.enabled true false allowed only under sanitize Restart audit.file $XDG_STATE_HOME/cui-proxy/decisions.jsonl if absolute; otherwise ~/.local/state/cui-proxy/decisions.jsonl Value-free decision log, private directory Restart audit.on_error warn under sanitize; block under strict Write-failure handling; strict requires block Restart for explicit setting changes audit.max_size_mb 50 Rotation size, 1–1048576; binary MiB Restart audit.retention_days 90 0–106751; 0 retains indefinitely; newest rotated file kept Restart observability.correlate false Optional process-local session/workspace pseudonyms in the metrics API; no payload retention Reload rules Empty list Rules below; not merged with starter rules Reload

The 64 KiB turn-metadata limit and JSON depth limit are not YAML options. Function-call argument restoration also has a fixed 20 MiB limit on cumulative argument delta input per response, and on each completed argument document. JSON tokens are buffered until complete so escaping and numeric boundaries can be restored correctly. Invalid or unfinished arguments cut the response stream; this does not change ordinary text streaming. Increasing max_body_bytes does not increase those limits.

docs.title: Rule fields
docs.text:
Field Applies to Meaning name All, required Unique rule name; recorded in diagnostics, so use category names rather than secrets type All, required builtin, dictionary, regex action All Omitted follows profile; sanitize or block; cannot weaken strict pattern Regex, required Go regexp syntax; whole match is masked, not just capture group 1; no lookaround/backreferences validate Regex, optional ipv4, ssn, luhn, or ocid; rejects invalid candidates; omitted means no extra validator file Dictionary, required Dictionary filename, relative to YAML directory or absolute synth Regex/dictionary, required Replacement class: ipv4, ipv6, cidr, hostname, email, ocid, ssn, card, secret

Built-in rules choose their own patterns and classes; pattern, validate, file and synth are not ways to customize that bundle. The bundle detects OCIDs, IPv4/IPv6/CIDR, address-plus-port tokens, emails, SSNs, card numbers, bearer tokens, JWTs and private-key blocks. It does not detect arbitrary usernames, repository paths or hostnames without suitable custom rules.

Dictionary files use one literal per line, ignore blank lines and lines starting with #, and match case-insensitively at alphanumeric boundaries. They are not regex files. A dictionary with no usable entries is rejected. Use synth: secret for opaque custom identifiers; choose address classes only when the matched value is a suitable address. A mischosen class can fail sanitization. All rules run: order is not an allow/block firewall list.

docs.title: Point Codex at the proxy
docs.text:
In ~/.codex/config.toml (or a profile):

model_provider = "cui-proxy"

[model_providers.cui-proxy]
name = "cui-proxy"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = true

Or for a single run:

codex -c 'model_provider="cui-proxy"' \
      -c 'model_providers.cui-proxy={name="cui-proxy",base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1",wire_api="responses",requires_openai_auth=true}'

requires_openai_auth = true makes Codex send its ChatGPT login headers to the proxy, which forwards them unchanged to the upstream.

The upstream mapping (/v1/responses -> https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses) passed a live smoke test on 2026-11-07 with Codex CLI 0.167.0 and gpt-6-astra, including streamed restoration and a shell tool round trip. See verification.md for evidence, scope, and repeatable checks.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Purpose init [-dir PATH] [-force] [-profile sanitize\|strict] Write a starter config.yaml and hosts.txt (mode 0600) into $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cui-proxy, else ~/.config/cui-proxy. Never overwrites without -force. policy init [-profile ...] / policy check -config PATH [-require-strict] init is the same as above; check validates the policy and says what is and is not enforced. menubar install\|uninstall\|status macOS only: build and manage the menu-bar app that runs the proxy in the background. info -config PATH Print the proxy and dashboard URLs for a config (used by the menu-bar app). serve -config PATH [-adapter codex] Run the proxy (default 127.0.0.1:8787) and the dashboard (default 127.0.0.1:8788). check-config -config PATH [-adapter NAME] Validate the config, rule files and selected adapter/upstream; prints ok: <N> rules, exits 1 on error. audit verify [-file PATH \| -config PATH] Check the decision log's hash chain across the active and rotated files; exit 1 on a break. explain [-config PATH] REQUEST-ID Say in plain words why a request was forwarded, sanitized or blocked, from the decision log. test-rules -config PATH Read stdin (max 8 MiB), print the sanitized text to stdout and a rule/class/count table to stderr. Uses a throwaway vault. version Print the version.

Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 failure, 2 usage error.

The upstream for ChatGPT-login Codex is configured in the proxy config:

upstreams:
  codex: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex

The upstream must be https (plain http is accepted only for a loopback host, for testing). See examples/config.yaml for the full, commented config. Relative dictionary and vault paths resolve against the config file's directory.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: http://127.0.0.1:8788/ shows the live request feed (rule names and counts, never values), metrics, the effective config, a "test a string" box, and a reload button. It is bound to localhost and refuses non-localhost Host headers and cross-origin POSTs.

docs.title: Hot reload
docs.text:
kill -HUP <pid> or the dashboard's reload button re-reads the config file and the dictionary files. The new rules apply only if the whole config is valid; otherwise the running rules stay and the error is shown. Requests already in flight finish with the rules they started with. The vault (and so every existing mapping) is kept.

Applied on reload: rules (and dictionary contents), policy.profile, policy.on_error, policy.max_body_bytes, observability.correlate. Need a restart (a reload logs WARN restart required for: ... and keeps the running values): listen, ui.listen, upstreams, vault.*, allow_non_loopback, all audit.* settings.

When audit failure handling was omitted, a profile change is not treated as an explicit audit-setting edit. Strict still forces audit failures to block. A reload to strict is refused if audit was disabled at startup; enable it and restart first. See decision-log.md for details.

SIGINT / SIGTERM stop the proxy with a 10 s drain for in-flight requests; a second signal closes at once.

docs.title: Vault
docs.text:
• vault.mode: memory (default): mappings live only in the process, under a random key that never touches disk. After a restart, synthetic values in history that Codex resends are unknown to the new vault and pass through unrestored.
  • vault.mode: file: mappings are stored encrypted (AES-256-GCM, file format CUIV2) in vault.file, keyed by vault.key_file (32 bytes, created with mode 0600 on first run; a key file with wider permissions is refused). The vault is saved every 30 s when it changed and on shutdown. A vault file that cannot be read (wrong key, missing key file, older format, corruption) stops startup; it is never silently replaced. To start over, remove the vault file yourself. Only one process may own a file vault: a lifetime lock prevents stale writers from overwriting mappings. Keep its parent directory private. A crash can still lose changes since the last periodic save.

docs.title: Synthetic address pool
docs.text:
IPv4 (and CIDR) synthetics come from the 762 RFC 5737 documentation addresses (192.0.2.x, 198.51.100.x, 203.0.113.x). When those are used up, the vault falls back to an overflow pool of 130,048 addresses in 198.18.0.0/15 (RFC 2544 benchmarking).

  • Exhaustion: when no synthetic is left, the request is blocked (HTTP 422, code sanitize, kind pool_exhausted; nothing is forwarded; see Block diagnostics). Mappings are never freed: the vault keeps growing for the life of the process (and of the vault file in file mode), and even a blocked request may have used up addresses.
  • Under policy.on_error: passthrough, exhaustion is a sanitize failure, so the original body, with its real IPs, can be forwarded. Successfully sanitized workspace metadata stays masked; metadata failures still block.
  • 198.18.0.0/15 can carry real traffic (lab and benchmark networks, and proxies or VPNs with a "fake-IP" mode). To keep a real address there from being confused with a synthetic: once the vault has seen any real address in that range, it stops coining overflow addresses (it then fails closed after the 762 RFC 5737 addresses); and a request containing an address that equals an existing overflow synthetic is blocked, because the proxy cannot tell whether it is real. Leading-zero spellings (198.018.001.001) count as the same address, and an IPv4/CIDR value that cannot be parsed also disables the overflow pool. In file mode this decision is saved with the vault and survives restarts. Each exact spelling still gets its own synthetic and restores byte for byte (some tools read leading-zero octets as octal); no synthetic ever equals any spelling of a known real. Residual risk: if your real traffic uses that range, expect blocks. A model reply that names a real 198.18.0.0/15 address the proxy has issued as a synthetic is restored to the wrong value.

docs.title: Maintain the documentation
docs.text: The published manual is built from docs/ with MkDocs Material. Markdown is reviewed in the same repository as the implementation. Changes to main automatically build and deploy to GitHub Pages. Pull requests build and validate the site without publishing.

docs.title: Preview locally
docs.text:
Use Python 3.12 or newer and the Go version specified in go.mod:

python3 -m venv .venv-docs
.venv-docs/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
go build -o bin/cui-proxy ./cmd/cui-proxy
.venv-docs/bin/python scripts/check-docs.py --binary bin/cui-proxy
.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs serve

Open the local URL printed by MkDocs. Before submitting:

.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs build --strict
git diff --check

Strict mode rejects broken local links, missing anchors, and navigation gaps. The executable check validates every YAML download with the real CLI and checks masking, blocking, dictionary boundaries, regex matches, and TOML syntax.

docs.title: Content conventions
docs.text:
• Put a new user guide in the relevant section of mkdocs.yml.
  • Explain the task and expected result before giving a command.
  • Label complete files versus partial edits. Use explicit filenames and tell the reader whether reload or restart is required.
  • Keep downloadable YAML in docs/examples/. Include it in code blocks with pymdownx.snippets so the displayed file and download cannot drift.
  • Use fabricated test data. Rule names, paths and regex patterns are visible in the dashboard, so review them before capturing screenshots.
  • Capture the actual dashboard in an isolated local demo. Hide all personal paths before the screenshot is written. Never publish real vaults, key files, dictionaries, tokens, or decision logs.
  • Keep the version statement and reference defaults consistent with source. Link dated test evidence as evidence, not a general compatibility promise.

Plans, specs, spikes, ADR proposals and raw verification records remain in the repository but are excluded from the site build. Link to their GitHub URLs when a current guide needs the historical context.

docs.title: Publishing and rollback
docs.text:
The site is versioned with mike. Every published version lives in its own folder of the gh-pages branch, which the Documentation workflow uploads as the Pages artifact; the branch is storage, not the Pages source. The repository's Pages setting must stay on GitHub Actions.

Event What is published Pull request Nothing. The build job validates the site, examples and offline manual. Push to main dev/, the guide for unreleased changes. Release tag vX.Y.Z vX.Y.Z/, and the latest/ alias moves to it. The site root redirects to latest/. The tag run then starts a second, main-branch run that uploads the site, because Pages serves only deployments made from a branch. Manual run Any version you name, optionally moving latest/. Use it to republish or to add a version that predates versioning. Tick sync_only to upload the gh-pages branch as it is without publishing anything.

The menu-bar app's Online Documentation item opens vX.Y.Z/ for the installed release, so a release's pages must exist: the tag push publishes them automatically. .github/workflows/docs.yml builds with read-only repository access; the publish job receives contents: write (to commit to gh-pages), the deploy job pages: write and id-token: write, and the tag handoff job actions: write (to start the main-branch upload). No personal access token is needed. The github-pages environment must allow deployments from main; the tag policy only lets the tag run publish.

To roll back a documentation change on dev, revert its commit through the normal review process. To fix a published release's pages, correct the source, then run the workflow by hand with that version. To remove a version entirely, run mike delete --push vX.Y.Z locally and rerun the workflow so the artifact matches the branch. The Go release workflow remains separate, so publishing the manual does not release a binary.

docs.title: Keep the bundled offline manual current
docs.text:
The menu-bar installer unpacks internal/manual/site.zip from the Go binary into the app before signing it. This committed generated artifact keeps normal go build, Homebrew and standalone binary installs independent of Python. mkdocs-offline.yml reuses the online theme and navigation with local HTML links, offline search, no repository widget, and a local iframe-worker shim. Diagrams remain readable source with adjacent prose; no CDN renderer is loaded. Third-party asset licenses are included in the archive.

After changing a published guide, example, screenshot, docs configuration or manual-build input, regenerate the snapshot with the pinned documentation tools:

.venv-docs/bin/python scripts/build-manual.py
go test ./internal/manual

Commit internal/manual/site.zip with the source changes. The Go test compares the full published-input list and SHA-256 digests against the embedded manifest, so stale or omitted source files fail CI and release tests. Historical excluded plans, specs, ADRs and raw evidence do not force a manual rebuild. The build is local and uses the vendored offline search shim in scripts/manual-assets/; reading the result makes no automatic external requests. Preview the extracted index.html as a file URL with networking disabled to check navigation, search, images and downloads. These checks are separate from the HTTP Pages preview.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard shows what the running proxy is doing and lets you test rules without sending a model request. Open http://localhost:8788/ with the default configuration. If you changed ui.listen, use the URL printed at startup or by:

cui-proxy info -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml

The proxy and dashboard use different ports: Codex connects to port 8787; your browser connects to port 8788. Start with the quick start or full tutorial if the proxy is not running yet.

Screenshots use an isolated source-build demo with fabricated data on ports 19787/19788; your configured ports and attachment mode may differ.

docs.title: Header and connection state
docs.text:
The header shows the binary version, active policy profile, and configured upstream URLs. config ok means the configuration endpoint was fetched; it does not prove that Codex is routed through the proxy or that the upstream is reachable. config unavailable means that fetch failed.

The status beside Live requests describes the event connection. It normally reads connected. A disconnected feed retries; if it eventually says live feed failed (reload the page), refresh the browser. Metrics refresh every two seconds independently of the feed.

docs.title: Metrics cards
docs.text:
Counters belong to the running process and reset on restart. Reloading rules does not reset them. Counts describe proxy activity, not the number of prompts or conversations: one client operation can generate several requests.

Card What it means Requests / min Requests received by the proxy during the last 60 seconds, including blocked requests. Requests Total requests received. The passthrough subcount is requests forwarded with their original body after an eligible sanitizer failure under policy.on_error: passthrough. Replacements Values replaced, with counts by detector rule. This counts transformation work, so replacements can occur even when a request is later refused.
