db.demo.example is masked; restricted-demo-project blocks. If one request contains both, the entire request blocks. A blocking rule wins even when its match overlaps a sanitizing rule. Reordering rules cannot create an exception.

docs.title: Keep mappings across restarts
docs.text:
Use a file vault when a conversation must retain its synthetic mappings across normal proxy restarts. The key and encrypted mapping file are both local.

persistent-vault.yaml — complete file
# Complete configuration. Save hosts.txt beside this file.
# Keep both vault files private and together; only one proxy may use this vault.
listen: localhost:8787
ui:
  listen: localhost:8788
upstreams:
  codex: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex
policy:
  profile: sanitize
  on_error: block
  unsupported: block
vault:
  mode: file
  key_file: .state/vault.key
  file: .state/vault.bin
audit:
  enabled: true
  file: .state/persistent-decisions.jsonl
  on_error: block
rules:
  - name: builtin
    type: builtin
  - name: service-hosts
    type: dictionary
    file: hosts.txt
    synth: hostname
  - name: aws-keys
    type: regex
    pattern: '\b(?:AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b'
    synth: secret
  - name: ticket-ids
    type: regex
    pattern: '\bDEMO-[0-9]{6}\b'
    synth: secret

The proxy creates missing state directories/files with private permissions. Keep the key and vault together in your private backup process; someone with both can recover the mappings. Only one proxy may use this vault at a time. Writes are periodic and on clean shutdown, so an abrupt crash can lose recent mappings. Do not delete or rotate the key while expecting old mappings to work.

test-rules still uses a throwaway vault even when given this configuration. It does not inspect or change the production file vault.

docs.title: Adapt a recipe for your environment
docs.text:
Need Change Check More hostnames Add literal lines to hosts.txt Positive and near-miss string tests, then reload Usernames, paths or project names Add a separate dictionary rule with synth: secret Built-ins do not cover arbitrary names/paths Your own identifier format Add a Go regex with a suitable synth Whole match is replaced; rule anatomy Different API/backend Change upstream and corresponding Codex authentication Restart; Codex setup A second isolated policy Separate YAML, ports, audit file and file vault Point that client at the correct local URL Larger request bodies Edit policy.max_body_bytes Does not raise fixed metadata/argument-stream limits

There is no per-value allowlist, built-in-category selector, per-request bypass, or automatic per-repository policy selection. A dictionary entry is a detection rule, not an approved destination. See supported overrides before trying to narrow a rule.

docs.title: Configuration and CLI reference
docs.text: This page is a lookup reference for the checked-out implementation. For a walkthrough, use configuration; for complete starting files, use recipes. Rules explains detection and overlap semantics, and policy explains blocking versus masking.

docs.title: Loading and paths
docs.text:
Configuration is one YAML document. Unknown fields and additional YAML documents are errors. check-config validates the YAML, synth classes, validators, dictionary files, selected adapter and all configured upstream URLs. It does not contact the upstream or prove a listener can bind, the vault can be opened, or the decision log can be written; those are startup checks.

Relative dictionary, vault, key and audit file paths resolve against the YAML file's directory, not your shell's current directory. ~ is not expanded inside YAML paths. Use a relative path or an actual absolute path there; shell commands in this manual use ~ where the shell expands it.

Defaults are loader defaults, not the content of init's starter file. In particular, the loader supplies neither an upstream nor rules. init writes a ChatGPT upstream and three rules: the built-in bundle, a dictionary, and an AWS-key regex. A sanitize configuration with no rules can validate and detects nothing; strict requires at least one rule.

docs.title: Fields and defaults
docs.text: Reload means save the file, then use the dashboard button or SIGHUP. Restart means stop and start the process. A successful reload keeps the running values of restart-only fields and logs a warning about changed fields. The dashboard shows the effective configuration.

docs.title: Listener and upstream fields
docs.text:
YAML field Loader default Accepted value and behavior Apply listen 127.0.0.1:8787 Proxy TCP address, normally loopback. Restart ui.listen 127.0.0.1:8788 Dashboard TCP address. Empty uses the default; it does not disable the UI. Restart allow_non_loopback false Allows non-loopback listener addresses. Adds neither TLS nor authentication. The macOS helper requires loopback. Restart upstreams Empty mapping Adapter name to base URL. The selected adapter must have an entry. Currently the registered adapter is codex. Restart upstreams.codex None Absolute HTTPS URL. Plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host for local testing. Credentials, query strings and fragments are rejected. Starter: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex. Restart

Loopback checks cover both the configured address and the address actually bound. localhost is accepted. Do not point Codex at the dashboard port; see Codex setup.

docs.title: Policy fields
docs.text:
YAML field Loader default Accepted value and behavior Apply policy.profile sanitize sanitize masks detections; strict blocks them. Rule actions may strengthen sanitize, but cannot weaken strict. Reload policy.on_error block block or passthrough. Passthrough can forward the original body on eligible sanitizer failures and is invalid with strict or any explicit blocking rule. It does not permit unsupported content or override policy matches. Reload policy.attachments block block or extract_text. From v0.4.0: supported inline PDF/PNG/JPEG becomes locally extracted text before scanning; original files never forwarded. All body failures block in extraction mode. See attachments. Reload policy.unsupported block Only block is accepted. Unsupported content is refused. Fixed behavior policy.max_body_bytes 20971520 (20 MiB) Maximum request body bytes. Negative is invalid; zero takes the default, not unlimited. Reload

No setting adds an allowlist, strict exception, approval workflow or action: allow. See limitations for supported content and credential exceptions.

docs.title: Vault fields
docs.text:
YAML field Loader default Accepted value and behavior Apply vault.mode memory memory or file. Memory mappings and their random key last only for the process. Restart vault.file Empty Required in file mode: encrypted mapping file. A damaged or unreadable existing vault stops startup rather than being overwritten. Restart vault.key_file Empty Required in file mode: 32-byte key file. Created with mode 0600 if no existing vault requires an existing key. Keys with broader permissions are refused. Restart

File mode uses AES-256-GCM and format CUIV2. It saves changed mappings every 30 seconds and on orderly shutdown; a crash can lose newer changes. One process holds a lifetime lock on the file vault. Keep the key, encrypted vault and parent directory private. Reload preserves the live mappings in either mode.

After a memory-mode restart, old synthetics in client history are unknown to the new vault and cannot be restored. Read architecture for mapping lifecycle and configuration for pool behavior.

docs.title: Audit fields
docs.text:
These configure the persistent decision log, distinct from the dashboard's in-memory request feed. All explicit audit field changes require restart.

YAML field Loader default Accepted value and behavior Apply audit.enabled true Boolean. false is rejected under strict. Restart audit.file $XDG_STATE_HOME/cui-proxy/decisions.jsonl when that environment variable is absolute; otherwise ~/.local/state/cui-proxy/decisions.jsonl Value-free decision-log path. An explicit relative path resolves beside the config. Restart audit.on_error warn under sanitize; block under strict warn continues when a decision cannot be written; block refuses the request. Strict rejects explicit warn. Restart for explicit changes audit.max_size_mb 50 Integer 1–1,048,576; rotation threshold in binary MiB despite the field name. Restart audit.retention_days 90 Integer 0–106,751. Zero retains rotated files indefinitely. The newest rotated file is kept. Restart

When audit.on_error is omitted, a profile-only reload does not count as an explicit audit edit; strict still forces failed writes to block. A reload to strict is refused if audit was disabled at startup. Enable logging and restart first. The hash chain detects damage under its documented limits; it is not proof against every form of tampering. See decision log.

docs.title: Rule fields
docs.text:
rules defaults to an empty list and is replaced as a whole when loaded. Every field below is part of the reloadable rule set. Dictionary contents are also reread on reload.

Field Required for Default / meaning name All rules No default. Nonempty, unique configuration name. Names appear in diagnostics; use category names, never sensitive values. type All rules No default. builtin, regex, or dictionary. action None Omitted follows profile. Explicit sanitize or block; sanitize is invalid under strict. pattern Regex Go regexp syntax. The entire match is masked, not a selected capture group. No lookaround or backreferences. validate None Regex candidate validator: ipv4, ssn, luhn, or ocid. Omitted means no additional validation. file Dictionary Literal dictionary file path. One entry per line; blank and # comment lines ignored. Empty usable dictionaries are rejected. synth Regex and dictionary Replacement class: ipv4, ipv6, cidr, hostname, email, ocid, ssn, card, or secret. No default.

A built-in bundle chooses its own patterns and classes. Its optional pattern, file, validator and synth fields do not customize that bundle; omit them. There is no selector to disable a single built-in detector. Dictionary matching is case-insensitive at alphanumeric boundaries. A synth class must suit the matched data; secret is appropriate for opaque identifiers.

All rules run. An overlapping block cannot be canceled by a sanitizing rule or by rule order. See rules for the built-in classes, span resolution, and examples.

docs.title: Reload, restart and signals
docs.text:
Operation Behavior Dashboard Reload config Reread the existing config path and rule files; swap policy/rules only after successful validation/build. kill -HUP PID Same reload operation. Replace PID with the running proxy process ID. Invalid reload Keep the old active rules and policy; daemon/dashboard diagnostics suppress parser details. Run check-config locally for details. Valid reload with restart-only changes Apply reloadable settings, preserve running restart-only settings, log WARN restart required for: …. In-flight request during reload Finish with its original policy/rule snapshot. Vault remains shared and retained. SIGINT or SIGTERM Stop with up to 10 seconds for in-flight requests to drain and save a file vault. Second stop signal during drain Cancel the drain and close promptly.

After upgrading a binary, restart the running service. Reload cannot load new program code. The menu-bar guide covers its managed process and binary selection.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Run cui-proxy help for the command list or cui-proxy COMMAND -h for command flags. Put flags before positional arguments. PATH, NAME, PID and REQUEST-ID below are placeholders.

Command and flags Purpose init [-dir PATH] [-force] [-profile sanitize\|strict] Write config.yaml and hosts.txt. Default profile is sanitize. Default directory is $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cui-proxy, otherwise ~/.config/cui-proxy. Does not overwrite without -force. policy init [-dir PATH] [-force] [-profile sanitize\|strict] Same starter generation as init. policy check -config PATH [-require-strict] Validate and summarize policy and its limits. -require-strict makes a non-strict config fail for scripts/audits. check-config -config PATH [-adapter NAME] Validate config, rule files and adapter/upstreams without forwarding traffic. Adapter default: codex. Prints ok: N rules on success. serve -config PATH [-adapter NAME] Run proxy and dashboard in the foreground. Adapter default: codex. Config is required. info -config PATH Print proxy and dashboard URLs from configuration; does not probe the running service. test-rules -config PATH Read at most 8 MiB from stdin. Write sanitized text to stdout and a rule/class/count table to stderr. Uses a throwaway vault and makes no upstream request. A policy match fails under strict or an applicable blocking rule. audit verify [-file PATH \| -config PATH] Verify the decision-log hash chain across active and rotated files. With neither flag, use the default log path. A broken chain exits 1. explain [-file PATH \| -config PATH] REQUEST-ID Read the decision log and explain one request. Uses the default log path if neither flag is given. The ID comes from errors, X-Cui-Proxy-Request-Id, or a dashboard row tooltip. menubar install [-config PATH] [-binary PATH] [-dir PATH] [-no-launch] macOS: compile/install CuiProxy.app and normally launch it. Default app directory: ~/Applications; default config: ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml; default binary: the one found on PATH. menubar status [-dir PATH] macOS: inspect the installed helper. menubar uninstall [-dir PATH] macOS: quit/remove the helper. Config, dictionary and logs remain. version Print the binary version. help, -h, -help, --help Print top-level usage.

Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for failure, and 2 for usage errors. The -file and -config log-selection flags are mutually exclusive. Use the same config as the running service when explaining requests.

Example local checks using only fabricated data:

cui-proxy check-config -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
cui-proxy policy check -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
printf '%s\n' 'Email demo.operator@example.com for the demo.' | cui-proxy test-rules -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml

The last command can fail intentionally under strict. Read testing for expected outcomes and verification for broader backend checks. The tutorial walks through the complete workflow.

docs.title: Local dashboard endpoints
docs.text:
These endpoints are on the dashboard listener, normally http://localhost:8788, not the proxy API. They are useful for local diagnosis; the dashboard is their primary client.

Method and path Response or effect GET / Embedded dashboard HTML. GET /healthz Plain text ok; dashboard reachability only, not upstream health. GET /api/config Effective configuration, version, rule definitions/actions and paths. No dictionary entries or vault values. GET /api/metrics Process counters, latency percentiles, vault size, uptime and live-feed drops as JSON. GET /api/events Recent in-memory request events, oldest first, up to 500. GET /api/stream Server-sent request events. A keepalive comment is sent every 15 seconds. POST /api/test JSON {"text":"…"}; returns sanitized text and rule/class/count entries using a throwaway vault. Limit: 1 MiB JSON request body. POST /api/reload Reload existing config; send JSON {}. Success: {"ok":true}. Validation failure: HTTP 422 with ok: false and an error.

For example, this read-only command checks the dashboard listener:

curl --fail http://localhost:8788/healthz

Non-loopback Host headers receive HTTP 421. Writes require Content-Type: application/json (optionally UTF-8 charset); wrong types receive 415. A supplied Origin must be HTTP with the same host and port, and supplied Sec-Fetch-Site must be same-origin or none; rejected cross-origin/site writes receive 403. There is no remote login or general CORS access.

The UI test returns HTTP 422 for policy blocks or transformation failures, 413 for an oversized request, and 400 for malformed JSON. Its exact UI messages and privacy boundaries are covered in dashboard. Do not expose these configuration and control endpoints publicly.

docs.title: Fixed limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Default request body limit 20 MiB; configurable with policy.max_body_bytes Attachment extraction per request (from v0.4.0) 8 attachments, 10 MiB decoded input, 20 total PDF pages, 2 MiB extracted text, 30 seconds; details Attachment images and processes (from v0.4.0) 16 million pixels per input image; PDF raster longest side 4000 pixels; 2 extraction processes globally Structured turn-metadata header 64 KiB; not a YAML option JSON nesting depth 64 levels; not a YAML option Function-call argument restoration 20 MiB cumulative argument-delta input per response and 20 MiB per completed argument document Dashboard test 1 MiB entire JSON body CLI test-rules 8 MiB stdin Dashboard browser rows / server recent events 200 / 500 Overhead samples Most recent 4,096

Increasing the body limit does not increase the other limits. Invalid or unfinished function-call argument documents terminate the response stream. See architecture, limitations and glossary for context.

docs.title: Workload observability
docs.text: observability.correlate defaults to false and can be changed by config reload. Enable it for temporary pseudonymous session/workspace records in /api/metrics. Stage timings and bounded gauges are always available. See the metrics API and correlation contract for fields, attribution limits and retention.

docs.title: Detection rules and replacements
docs.text:
A rule answers two questions: what text should be detected, and what should happen when it matches. Under the default sanitize profile, matches are replaced with local vault synthetics. Under strict, they reject the request. A rule can also explicitly block under sanitize.

Use the configuration walkthrough for the edit/validate/ reload cycle, recipes for complete files, and the reference for settings outside the rules list.

docs.title: Rule anatomy
docs.text:
This is a partial YAML edit: add the entry to your existing rules list.

rules:
  - name: project-tickets
    type: regex
    pattern: 'DEMO-[0-9]{6}'
    synth: secret
    action: sanitize

It masks the entire DEMO-123456 match under sanitize. Remove the explicit action before using this entry in a strict configuration.

Field Applies to Meaning name All; required Unique rule name. Appears in diagnostics and logs, so use a category name, never a sensitive value type All; required builtin, regex, or dictionary action All; optional sanitize or block; omitted inherits policy.profile. Explicit sanitize is invalid under strict pattern Regex; required Go regular expression; the whole match is selected validate Regex; optional Additional candidate validator: ipv4, ssn, luhn, or ocid file Dictionary; required Literal entries, one per line. Relative paths resolve from the YAML file's directory synth Regex/dictionary; required Replacement class from the table below. Built-ins supply their own classes

Use fields for their applicable rule type: synth does not change built-in classes, and validate is not a general post-filter for the built-in bundle or dictionaries. Unknown YAML field names are rejected. Rules are loaded from the one selected YAML file; there is no automatic merge with starter rules. Omitting rules does not enable built-ins. Sanitize can validate with no rules and then detect nothing; strict requires at least one.

docs.title: The built-in bundle
docs.text:
This partial YAML edit enables the complete bundle:

rules:
  - name: builtin
    type: builtin

Its detector names use <name>.<class>, such as builtin.email. Multiple secret detectors share builtin.secret. It is one bundle: there is no individual built-in category toggle, exclusion list, or per-value allowlist.

Category What it looks for Important detail ocid Oracle Cloud identifiers Checks OCID structure ipv4 IPv4 literals Validates addresses rather than accepting every dotted digit sequence ipv6 IPv6 literals Parses address candidates, including supported embedded address forms cidr IPv4/IPv6 address prefixes Includes the prefix length in the detected span email Email-shaped text Can match the user/host portion of an SSH remote ssn Dashed US Social Security number shapes Applies validity checks; a synthetically invalid 000 area is not a real SSN detector sample card Separated card-like digit sequences Uses Luhn validation and supported length checks secret Tokens using the Bearer scheme, JWT-shaped tokens, private-key blocks, selected numeric runs and address/port tokens The bearer-token detector requires at least eight token characters; an unterminated private-key block is masked to end of text

Unseparated card-like digit runs and long numeric IDs containing a Luhn hit are masked as opaque secrets rather than preserving a card shape. Tcpdump-style dotted address/port tokens are masked whole, including the port. Five single-digit dotted components are treated as a version number, not an address/port token.

The built-ins do not include AWS access-key IDs. The starter configuration adds this separate rule (partial YAML edit):

rules:
  - name: aws-keys
    type: regex
    pattern: '\b(?:AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b'
    synth: secret

This detects key-ID shapes, not every AWS credential or secret-key format. For OCI configuration fields and AWS credential assignments, use the OCI and AWS CLI rules guide and its complete recipe. General hostnames, local paths, usernames, and names specific to your organization need your own rules. A hostname that encodes an address is not an IP literal. See limitations.

docs.title: Custom regular expressions
docs.text:
Patterns use Go's RE2-style regexp syntax. Alternation, character classes, repetition, and flags such as (?i) are available. Lookaround and backreferences are not. Use single-quoted YAML strings so a backslash reaches the regex engine unchanged.

The entire regex match is replaced, not capture group 1. For example, ticket=(DEMO-[0-9]{6}) masks ticket=DEMO-123456, including the label. Use DEMO-[0-9]{6} if only the identifier should be replaced. The built-in bearer-token detector has special internal handling for its token capture; custom rules do not inherit it.

Validators reject candidates that fail their check; they do not change the rule's action or automatically choose a replacement class. Match only the value expected by the selected validator, and choose a compatible synth. For arbitrary identifiers, secret is the simplest replacement class.

Test both positive and negative cases. A regex that looks useful on one line may overmatch JSON tool output or an ordinary protocol identifier when you enable blocking. The testing guide explains local tests and their limits.

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text:
A dictionary is a local text file of literal sensitive names. This is a complete example dictionary file, using fabricated names:

# demo-names.txt
demo-customer
demo-build-host

Connect it with this partial YAML edit:

rules:
  - name: demo-names
    type: dictionary
    file: demo-names.txt
    synth: hostname

Blank lines and lines beginning with # after trimming are ignored. Leading and trailing whitespace is removed. Entries are literal, not regex patterns; matching is case-insensitive, duplicate entries are removed, and longer entries are tried first. At an alphanumeric edge, the entry cannot be glued to an adjacent alphanumeric character. Punctuation is not a general word boundary: test the exact forms you expect to send.

An empty dictionary is rejected when detectors are built. Relative paths use the YAML directory, not your shell's current directory; ~ inside YAML is not expanded. Reload after editing the file. Adding a name increases detection; a dictionary is not an allowlist.

docs.title: Replacement classes
docs.text:
synth chooses an output shape, not a detector. Setting synth: email does not make an arbitrary regex validate email addresses. Shapes help the model work with a value's role, but replacements need not preserve its exact format or remain meaningful to external tools.

Class Replacement behavior and limits secret Opaque REDACTED- token followed by eight hexadecimal characters; useful for arbitrary identifiers hostname Hash-derived h-….example hostname email Hash-derived user-…@mail.example address ocid ocid1.<type>.ocsynth..…; retains a valid resource-type token when possible, otherwise uses resource ipv4 Starts with the three RFC 5737 documentation blocks; after that finite pool is exhausted, may use the RFC 2544 benchmarking range ipv6 Address in the IPv6 documentation prefix cidr Generates an IPv4-shaped address and retains the source prefix-length number; does not preserve IPv6 family or network topology ssn Dashed shape with area 000, deliberately invalid as a real SSN card Replaces digits, retaining separators; starts with 400000 and computes a Luhn check digit. Generator accepts 8–19 digits; this is not a usable payment credential

CIDR replacements are textual stand-ins. In particular, an IPv6 prefix length can exceed the valid length for the generated IPv4 shape. Do not treat them as operational network definitions or assume subnet relationships survive.

The IPv4 documentation pool has 762 addresses. The overflow pool can carry real traffic in laboratory or fake-IP environments; it is not guaranteed to be non-real. The vault stops allocating overflow addresses after observing a real value in that range. A detected value equal to an overflow synthetic can block rather than pass as already sanitized. Pools and collision retries are finite; allocation failures block with the default policy.

Broad CIDRs, including default routes, can still use documentation-address replacements when overflow allocation is disabled. A replacement's address determines its pool; its prefix length does not. Real prefixes overlapping the overflow range continue to disable overflow allocation.

Mappings are stable within the same vault. A new memory vault after a restart does not retain the previous mapping. File mode retains mappings encrypted locally. See architecture.

docs.title: When a replacement becomes an opaque token
docs.text:
The sanitizer verifies that its output restores faithfully in its surrounding text. Some classes use boundaries to avoid accidental restoration inside unrelated text. If a replacement would land against neighboring characters that make those boundaries fail, the offending span is retried as secret. Its audit event has downgraded: true; this changes the output shape, not the policy action. A failed restoration check after that retry still blocks.

Overlapping detections also affect output shape: the merged union uses the winning member's class, which may cover more text than that member originally matched. If that class cannot generate or restore the merged value safely, the request can be refused. Choose secret for broad custom patterns whose values do not have a predictable shape.

docs.title: Precedence, overlaps, and actions
docs.text:
Rules are not a first-match firewall. Every detector runs. Overlapping spans are merged transitively into their full union; spans that only touch stay separate. The representative rule/class is chosen by longest match, then earliest start, then class specificity (ocid, cidr, other classes, ipv4), then detector input order for an exact tie.

A block always survives merging. If a short blocking rule overlaps a longer sanitizing rule, the entire request is rejected. Reordering the list does not allow the sanitizing rule to cancel that decision.

Profile Omitted action action: block action: sanitize sanitize Mask and restore Reject whole request Mask and restore strict Reject whole request Reject whole request Invalid configuration

When any rule blocks, protocol fields normally preserved without scanning are also checked against blocking rules, without rewriting. Known protocol include constants remain unscanned; unknown include strings are inspected. The ciphertext exception remains. Headers and query fields that cannot be rewritten block on any detection, even under sanitize. Unsupported content always blocks.

Any blocking rule requires policy.on_error: block. Passthrough does not override a policy match and is not an allowlist. There is no allow, exclude, per-request exception, account allowlist, or verified approval mechanism in the current implementation. Strict requires enabled auditing with audit failure set to block. See policy profiles.

Validate configuration, try fabricated text in test-rules or the dashboard, then reload. A failed reload keeps the old rules. Use the decision log and troubleshooting guide to find the effective rule behind a block. For a complete first run, use the quick start or tutorial.

docs.title: Test your setup
docs.text:
Test in layers. A YAML parser, a string preview, and a live Codex round trip answer different questions. Use fabricated values throughout so the test itself does not expose real information.

Layer What it proves What it does not prove check-config YAML, rule files, supported classes and upstream configuration load Running process uses that file; upstream works policy check Effective profile and configured restrictions Organizational approval or complete coverage test-rules / dashboard preview Detection and policy for that text HTTP/metadata parsing, credentials, routing or stream restoration Dashboard health/config Local UI responds and reports active configuration Model backend is reachable Live synthetic Codex run Routing and the tested model-response path Every payload type or future client version Tool round trip Tested tool-output and argument restoration path All tools, permissions or external destinations

docs.title: 1. Validate the file you actually use
docs.text:
cui-proxy version
cui-proxy check-config -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
cui-proxy policy check -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
cui-proxy info -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml

Use your installation's actual path. info reads a file; it does not prove the running service loaded it. Compare the dashboard's effective configuration and startup log after reload/restart.

docs.title: 2. Build a small positive and negative test set
docs.text:
For the downloadable masking recipe, these are useful cases:

Fabricated text Expected under sanitize Expected under strict db.demo.example Dictionary match, masked Blocked DB.DEMO.EXAMPLE Case-insensitive dictionary match Blocked xdb.demo.examplex No dictionary match at alphanumeric boundaries Unchanged if no other rule matches 203.0.113.42 Built-in address match, masked Blocked DEMO-123456 Custom ticket regex match Blocked DEMO-12345 No ticket regex match Unchanged if no other rule matches Explain retry backoff Unchanged Unchanged 
printf '%s\n' 'Check db.demo.example at 203.0.113.42 for DEMO-123456' |
  cui-proxy test-rules -config /path/to/recipe/config.yaml

For a masking result, stdout contains the transformed text and stderr contains rule/class/count rows. Strict or explicit blocking rules produce failure without forwarding anything. Expected rule names depend on your YAML. The stock starter does not contain the tutorial's ticket rule.

Use the same samples in Test a string. A new throwaway vault is used each time, so compare the rule names, counts and remaining text rather than an exact synthetic spelling. “No matches” only describes the configured detectors and that input; it does not mean the text is safe.

docs.title: 3. Check local service availability
docs.text:
curl -fsS http://localhost:8788/healthz

Expect ok. For the tutorial instance use port 18788. This endpoint belongs to the dashboard, not the model-facing listener. Open the UI and check its profile, upstream, listeners and rule actions. Start with troubleshooting if they differ from your intended settings.

docs.title: 4. Verify routing and response restoration
docs.text:
Launch Codex using the one-session command and submit:

Reply with 203.0.113.42 exactly. Do not run tools.

After completion, check:

  1. A POST /v1/responses row appears in this proxy's dashboard.
  2. Address-rule replacements increase. Other client context may also match.
  3. If the model echoes the value, the client sees the original fabricated address and restore counts increase.
  4. The decision record says sanitized (or blocked under strict), with rule names and counts but no raw text.

The feed only gets a row when the request finishes. A model may not follow an exact-echo instruction; inspect the evidence before concluding restoration is broken. The UI does not expose the upstream body. For wire-level evidence, follow the controlled, synthetic backend verification procedure.

docs.title: 5. Verify a harmless tool round trip
docs.text:
Use a new conversation through the proxy and ask:

Run printf '%s\n' '203.0.113.42' in the shell, then repeat its output exactly.
Do not contact any host or change any files.

If your Codex execution policy allows the command, this exercises restored tool arguments, local execution, sanitization of tool output in the next request, and the final streamed reply. Inspect the executed command and final output in your client. Permission denial is a separate client/tool issue; it does not prove a proxy policy block.

For JSON/newline and workspace metadata regressions, use the specific cases in verification evidence. Do not replace them with a single plain-text preview: they test different parser paths.

docs.title: 6. Check strict or selective blocking
docs.text:
Use an isolated config such as the tutorial to avoid changing a live session unexpectedly. A string matching a blocking rule should fail in the preview. A matching complete request should receive a value-free 422 diagnostic. Check the request ID with:

cui-proxy explain -config /path/to/config.yaml REQUEST-ID
cui-proxy audit verify -config /path/to/config.yaml

Some guards, such as malformed metadata or an unknown route, block independently of rule matches. See Block diagnostics.

docs.title: Check attachment conversion (from v0.4.0)
docs.text:
test-rules and the dashboard text box do not invoke PDF extraction or OCR. After building/upgrading to a binary that supports attachments, check the effective setting and use fabricated inline documents with a controlled fake upstream. Confirm that it receives only sanitized input_text, with no file_data, image_url, filename, or original sensitive test value. Under strict, the same detected value must block with no upstream call. Also test disabled mode, file IDs/URLs, invalid data and missing tools; inspect explain REQUEST-ID.

Repository tests cover this boundary with real Poppler when installed, and controlled OCR executables for deterministic invocation/failure checks. Actual OCR quality and the client wire format require separate deployment verification.

docs.title: After edits and upgrades
docs.text:
Repeat the local samples whenever you change rules. After a binary/client/model upgrade, restart the running proxy and repeat the routing, streaming and tool checks. Record versions and synthetic cases that passed. Preserve a working configuration backup so a failed rule edit can be reverted and reloaded.

The repository runs executable checks of its downloadable examples and a strict documentation build in CI. This validates the examples; it does not replace testing your own dictionaries, network environment or backend account.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
First identify the failing layer: configuration/startup, the local dashboard, a proxy policy decision, the model upstream, or a local tool such as Git. A policy block and a broken SSH login need different fixes.

Use fabricated input when reproducing a problem. Keep raw prompts, credential headers, dictionary entries, vault files and keys out of reports. Rule names, regex patterns and paths can also reveal information; inspect diagnostics and screenshots before sharing them.

docs.title: Establish the active setup
docs.text:
Run these local commands with the config used by your service:

cui-proxy version
cui-proxy check-config -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
cui-proxy policy check -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
cui-proxy info -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml

check-config is deliberately more detailed than daemon errors and can quote configuration text. info reports configured URLs; it does not prove a process is listening there. Open the dashboard to inspect the running version, profile, rule actions and effective settings. An installed new binary does not replace an old running process: restart after upgrades. On macOS, check the menu-bar helper's binary and config selection too.

If a proxy response contains a request ID, look up its decision:

cui-proxy explain -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml REQUEST-ID

Use the 16-character hexadecimal ID from the error, response header or dashboard row tooltip. See decision log and block diagnostics for the evidence and reason codes.

docs.title: Startup and configuration
docs.text:
Symptom Diagnosis Fix configuration or rule files could not be loaded The daemon hides parser details to avoid logging values. YAML, a regex, a synth/validator, or a dictionary may be invalid. Run check-config locally on the same file, correct its detailed error, and retry. Use reference for accepted fields. Unknown field or unexpected YAML document Misspelled key, unsupported option, or more than one YAML document. Keep one document and use only supported fields. There is no allow, exclude or action: allow. Dictionary not found, or has no entries Relative paths are based on the YAML directory; blank and comment-only dictionaries are invalid. Put the literal file beside the config or use its actual absolute path. Add fabricated entries for tests. YAML does not expand ~. no upstream configured for adapter "codex" Loader defaults do not supply an upstream. Use a complete recipe, or add the appropriate upstreams.codex to your existing config. Upstream URL validation error Non-absolute URL, embedded credentials, query/fragment, unsupported scheme, or non-loopback plain HTTP. Use an absolute HTTPS base URL. Plain HTTP is for loopback fake upstreams only. Authentication belongs in client headers. Bind/listen failure or address already in use Another process owns the proxy or UI port, or the address cannot bind. Stop the duplicate instance, or choose two unused loopback ports and update Codex routing. Restart for listener changes. Avoid running a manual server alongside the menu-bar managed server. Non-loopback address refused Listener validation or the actual bound-address check rejected it. Use localhost or a loopback literal. allow_non_loopback is an explicit exposure override, not a routine fix or authentication layer. Strict configuration rejected It has no rules, explicit action: sanitize, passthrough, disabled audit, or audit warning mode. Keep at least one rule, remove weakening settings, and use enabled audit with block-on-error. See policy. File vault is locked Another proxy owns that file. Stop the other owner or use a separate vault for a separate instance. Do not share one writable vault across processes. Existing vault cannot open Missing/wrong key, broad key permissions, corruption, or incompatible format. Restore the matching key/vault pair and private permissions. Do not generate a replacement key for an existing vault. See configuration.

Start from the quick start or tutorial if a custom file is difficult to reason about. Compare against a complete recipe rather than pasting a partial YAML block over an entire configuration.

docs.title: Dashboard and reload
docs.text:
Symptom Diagnosis Fix Browser cannot connect Wrong port, proxy process stopped, or changed ui.listen. Use the startup dashboard URL. Default UI port is 8788; proxy port is 8787. Test curl --fail http://localhost:8788/healthz for the default listener. config ok but no traffic Config fetch succeeded, but Codex might bypass the proxy, no request has completed, or the feed disconnected. Check Codex provider setup, effective proxy URL and feed status. Streaming requests appear only when they finish. config unavailable Browser cannot fetch the dashboard config endpoint. Verify the local listener and reload the page. Use a localhost URL, without a remote dashboard wrapper or rewritten Host. reconnecting... or live feed failed (reload the page) The event connection was interrupted. Refresh the page; verify the process remains running. Feed drops mean slow event consumers, not failed durable writes. reload failed with generic rule-file error New YAML or detector build failed; old rules remain active. Run check-config, fix the file and reload again. Reload says success but port/upstream/vault/audit did not change Those fields are restart-only and pinned to their running values. Restart, then inspect the effective panel. Check daemon warnings listing fields requiring restart. Reload to strict refused because audit was disabled Reload cannot open a log disabled at startup. Set audit.enabled: true and restart with a valid strict configuration. Dictionary or regex edit has no effect Disk edits are not automatically watched, or you edited another file. Validate the actual service config, reload and inspect the displayed rule/path/action. Built-in row has empty Synth and Pattern / file Expected: the bundle supplies its own patterns/classes. Test a fabricated built-in match; do not fill those cells to customize the bundle. See rules. HTTP 421, 403 or 415 from a dashboard endpoint Host, cross-origin/site, or JSON-content-type guard rejected the request. Open the dashboard directly through localhost. Local API writes need JSON and same-origin conditions; see reference.

The dashboard is local and has no login. Keep it on loopback. It displays configuration paths and patterns, so screenshot privacy still matters even though the live request feed contains metadata rather than prompt values.

docs.title: Unexpected rule-test results
docs.text:
Use Test a string or the local CLI before involving a model backend:

printf '%s\n' 'Send the demo report to demo.operator@example.com.' | cui-proxy test-rules -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml
Symptom Diagnosis Fix no matches or unchanged text No loaded detector recognizes that value, a regex boundary differs, or the test uses old rules. Confirm the effective rule, reload edits, and test positive/negative fabricated examples. Built-ins are not general username/hostname/path detectors. UI says error: blocked by policy (rule=…, class=…) Strict or explicit action: block matched. This is expected behavior. Remove the sensitive value from the request or adjust a custom policy only if masking is acceptable. No strict per-value override exists. Broad match or unexpected count Full regex matches and overlap resolution differ from intended capture groups; multiple rules ran. Test punctuation/adjacency/repeats, narrow the custom regex, and read rule semantics. A blocking overlap always wins. text could not be sanitized reversibly A match cannot be transformed safely, including an unsuitable synth class or ambiguous input. Reproduce with fabricated data and inspect pattern/class. Use secret for opaque identifiers. Do not bypass the failure by enabling passthrough. UI text too large The JSON body exceeded 1 MiB, including escaping overhead. Use smaller samples or test-rules for at most 8 MiB stdin. These are separate from the proxy request-body limit. Synthetics differ between tests Each test uses a new random-key throwaway vault. Assert masking, class and count rather than a fixed synthetic spelling. Test passes but a real request blocks Plain-text tests do not exercise request structure, metadata, headers, routing or response streams. Follow testing and verification with a fabricated full request.

Neither a successful rule test nor no matches guarantees that a request has no sensitive content. Detection is limited to configured rules and supported representations; read limitations.

docs.title: Proxy refusals and upstream failures
docs.text:
The error's reason, kind, rule, optional detail, and request ID narrow the diagnosis. A metadata header error does not identify a particular header by itself.

Symptom / code Diagnosis Fix policy / rule_match A body detection has effective action block. Check active profile and named rule. Remove the value or change policy only when your requirements permit masking. header / rule_match or bad_body Strict metadata detection, a match in an unchanged field/header/query, or malformed structured turn metadata. Reproduce with fabricated workspace metadata and verify the current binary. Supported workspaces/cwd masking does not make every header rewritable. route Unsupported method/path. Use the documented Codex Responses provider setup and supported routes; arbitrary API traffic is not automatically supported. compressed Request body encoding cannot be inspected. Send uncompressed supported JSON. There is no unsupported-content bypass. body_too_large Request body exceeds configured limit. Reduce context/request size, or deliberately adjust policy.max_body_bytes and reload. Other fixed limits remain. sanitize / bad_body Invalid JSON/UTF-8, unsupported content, or unsupported structure. Remove images/files/audio or other unsupported input and reproduce with synthetic text-only content. Check limitations; do not use passthrough as a fix. sanitize / depth JSON nesting exceeds 64 levels. Simplify nested data. Increasing the byte limit does not change this bound. sanitize / pseudonym A detected value does not suit its synth class. Correct the custom rule or validator and test fabricated cases. sanitize / pool_exhausted A synthetic pool is exhausted. Review configuration's pool limits and vault lifecycle. A planned fresh vault loses old restoration mappings; do not delete a live vault casually. sanitize / ambiguous A value conflicts with an issued overflow synthetic. Review the documented overflow-pool restriction. Preserve fail-closed behavior; capture only fabricated reproductions. unrestorable A safe reversible transformation could not be achieved. Keep the refusal, record rule/kind/version and reproduce with fabricated input for a private security report if appropriate. audit with HTTP 503 Required decision record could not be written. Inspect log directory permissions, available disk space and decision-log health. Restore writeability; keep strict logging enabled. HTTP 502 upstream The proxy could not complete the upstream request. Check intended HTTPS upstream, network/VPN and authentication environment. A local rule test cannot validate connectivity. HTTP 502 upstream_redirect Upstream returned a redirect which the proxy refuses to relay. Correct the upstream base URL rather than relying on redirects. stream_rewrite, cut stream, or apparent 200 followed by failure Unsupported/encoded response format or restoration failed after streaming began. Use a supported SSE Responses backend. Check value-free daemon diagnostics and fabricate a reproduction; initial HTTP status alone cannot prove stream success. Upstream 401/403 Client credentials or backend permissions may be wrong. Confirm the chosen provider and login configuration; the proxy passes designated authentication headers unchanged. Do not paste those headers into reports.

policy.on_error: passthrough is unsafe for original bodies and is not a universal unblock switch. It cannot coexist with strict or explicit blocking rules, and does not override metadata failures, policy detections, unsupported content or size/depth limits. See policy and block diagnostics.

docs.title: Git and SSH are separate from model routing
docs.text:
Codex sends model requests through cui-proxy. A local git command opens its own network connection. The proxy does not authorize shell commands or open, filter, or approve the SSH socket. It can still block the model request containing a remote URL, proposed command, or earlier tool output.

What you see Investigate Appropriate fix Proxy HTTP 422 with rule=builtin.email around a fabricated SSH remote such as demo.operator@example.com:demo/repo.git Model-request content and effective action. An email-like SSH user/host can match the email detector. Supported text and workspace fields can be masked under sanitize; strict and blocking rules still refuse matches. Test the fabricated remote locally and use explain. Permission denied (publickey) SSH key, agent environment, GitHub identity and repository access. Repair SSH authentication/authorization. Proxy YAML has no SSH allowlist. DNS failure, connection timeout/refused Network, VPN, firewall and SSH endpoint. Diagnose the local Git/SSH network path. Agent command approval or sandbox denial Execution and network permissions of the agent. Use the supported approval flow for the intended command; a proxy profile cannot grant it. non-fast-forward Git branch history. Fetch and reconcile branch state according to the repository workflow.

A read-only git ls-remote origin tests remote access from the same repository; it contacts the remote and may require agent network permission. If it works in your terminal but fails in an agent, compare SSH-agent environment and execution permissions. Do not change transport or disable detectors merely to fix a different layer.

For the escaped-newline-before-match sanitize:bad_body defect in v0.3.2 and earlier, use v0.3.3 or later and restart the running proxy. SSH key changes, disabling email detection and enabling passthrough do not repair that parser issue. See configuration for the historical context and verification for regression scope.

docs.title: PDF, image and file refusals
docs.text:
422 reason=sanitize kind=bad_body is a body validation failure, independent of the number of blocking rules. Attachments are blocked by default. The text extraction mode converts supported inline PDF/PNG/JPEG content locally; it never forwards originals.

New errors add fixed details such as attachment_file_disabled, attachment_file_reference, or attachment_image_missing_tool, with a remedy in the response and server log. explain REQUEST-ID reads the persisted detail. An old record without a detail cannot reveal the exact cause retroactively. For tool failures, check the service PATH and English Tesseract data; a terminal installation alone does not prove a menu-bar process can find the executable. A v0.3.3 binary rejects the new setting: upgrade/build and restart first.

docs.title: Decision-log and restoration questions
docs.text:
If explain reports no record, confirm the log path, whether audit was enabled, and whether retention removed the relevant segment. The UI's recent events are not a permanent substitute. A failed log write can also leave no persistent record. Run:

cui-proxy audit verify -config ~/.config/cui-proxy/config.yaml

A broken chain is evidence to investigate, not an invitation to edit the log. Strict/block-on-error startup refuses damaged logs; sanitize warning mode can start a new segment. See decision log for recovery and verification limits.

If a model echoes synthetics after a restart, check whether you used memory mode or switched vaults. Old mappings are gone in memory mode. File mode needs the same readable vault and key. If response text invents or changes a token, exact restoration may also be impossible; see architecture and glossary.

For a useful report, include the binary version, fabricated minimal input, profile/effective rule action, error reason/kind, and which local or end-to-end check reproduced it. Share no real sensitive values. Report suspected bypasses through the repository's private vulnerability-reporting process.

docs.title: Repeated policy blocks after reading a fixture
docs.text:
A fabricated identifier or credential example can match an explicit blocking rule. If a tool prints it into a proxied assistant session, the next request can fail with HTTP 422, reason=policy kind=rule_match. Retrying can repeat the failure because conversation history includes the same tool output.

Reproduce with cui-proxy test-rules locally, capture stdout and stderr, and report only the status and rule name. Keep matching fixtures and full config responses out of the session. Start a fresh session if the existing history contains the trigger, and avoid reading that fixture back into it. Preserve intentional blocking rules. See the active-policy verification check.

docs.title: End-to-end configuration tutorial
docs.text:
Use this walkthrough to learn the whole edit → validate → preview → reload → verify cycle. The scenario is a fictional service with a database host and internal ticket IDs. Every sample is fabricated.

You will finish with: a separate test configuration, a working dictionary and custom rule, a Codex session routed through it, and a strict-policy check. The tutorial uses ports 18787 / 18788, separate from the usual 8787 / 8788.

docs.title: 1. Create an isolated configuration directory
docs.text:
Install the binary using the quick start if necessary. In a terminal, run:

cui_demo_dir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/cui-tutorial.XXXXXX")
curl -fsSL https://rozdolsky33.github.io/cui-proxy/examples/tutorial.yaml \
  -o "$cui_demo_dir/config.yaml"
curl -fsSL https://rozdolsky33.github.io/cui-proxy/examples/hosts.txt \
  -o "$cui_demo_dir/hosts.txt"
chmod 600 "$cui_demo_dir/config.yaml" "$cui_demo_dir/hosts.txt"
printf 'Tutorial directory: %s\n' "$cui_demo_dir"

Keep this terminal open: $cui_demo_dir refers to your new directory. You can also download tutorial.yaml and hosts.txt manually. Save the YAML as config.yaml beside the dictionary. The directory contains only tutorial state; none of these steps overwrites your normal setup.

docs.title: 2. Understand the complete file
docs.text:
config.yaml — complete tutorial configuration
# Complete isolated tutorial configuration. Save hosts.txt beside this file.
listen: localhost:18787
ui:
  listen: localhost:18788
upstreams:
  codex: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex
policy:
  profile: sanitize
  on_error: block
  unsupported: block
vault:
  mode: memory
audit:
  enabled: true
  file: .state/tutorial-decisions.jsonl
  on_error: block
rules:
  - name: builtin
    type: builtin
  - name: service-hosts
    type: dictionary
    file: hosts.txt
    synth: hostname
  - name: aws-keys
    type: regex
    pattern: '\b(?:AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}\b'
    synth: secret
  - name: ticket-ids
    type: regex
    pattern: '\bDEMO-[0-9]{6}\b'
    synth: secret

The pieces have separate jobs:

  1. listen receives Codex model traffic; ui.listen serves the dashboard.
  2. upstreams.codex is the destination the proxy forwards to. It is different from the local URL configured in Codex.
  3. policy.profile: sanitize masks detections. Both failure-handling settings remain block.
  4. vault.mode: memory keeps reversible mappings until this process stops.
  5. audit.on_error: block requires a decision record before forwarding. This recipe deliberately uses a stronger audit setting than the default starter.
  6. Four rules enable built-ins, your dictionary, AWS-key patterns, and ticket IDs.

docs.title: 3. Validate and preview
docs.text:
cui-proxy check-config -config "$cui_demo_dir/config.yaml"
cui-proxy policy check -config "$cui_demo_dir/config.yaml"
printf '%s\n' 'Check db.demo.example at 203.0.113.42 for DEMO-123456' |
  cui-proxy test-rules -config "$cui_demo_dir/config.yaml"

Expect ok: 4 rules, a description of the sanitize policy, and three replaced values in the text. The count table should name service-hosts, builtin.ipv4, and ticket-ids. Exact stand-ins vary because each test uses a new temporary vault. No upstream service is contacted by these commands.

docs.title: 4. Start and inspect
docs.text:
cui-proxy serve -config "$cui_demo_dir/config.yaml"

Open http://localhost:18788/. Confirm the header says profile: sanitize, the listeners end in 18787 / 18788, and the rules table has all four entries. Paste the previous test text into Test a string and click Sanitize. See Dashboard walkthrough for the expected display.

docs.title: 5. Extend your dictionary without restarting
docs.text:
Open the tutorial hosts.txt in your editor and add a new line:

cache.demo.example

In the dashboard, try Check cache.demo.example before reloading. The running service still has the old dictionary, so this name remains unchanged. Click Reload config, confirm reload ok, and test again. The new name should now become a synthetic hostname. The dictionary is a file loaded into memory; editing it alone does not update a running service.

For normal operation, run check-config with the actual path before reloading. A reload error keeps the previous valid configuration active. Changes to listeners, upstreams, vault, or explicit audit settings need a restart.

docs.title: 6. Prove a request reaches this proxy
docs.text:
In a second terminal, launch a temporary Codex session:

codex -c 'model_provider="cui-tutorial"' \
  -c 'model_providers.cui-tutorial={name="cui-tutorial",base_url="http://localhost:18787/v1",wire_api="responses",requires_openai_auth=true,supports_websockets=false}'

Use the model already available in your Codex account. Submit:

Repeat this line exactly without running tools:
Check db.demo.example at 203.0.113.42 for DEMO-123456

After it completes, inspect the dashboard's live feed and replacement/restore counts. If the model repeated the stand-ins unchanged, your client should show the original fabricated values. A model can paraphrase or omit text; use the verification guide to distinguish model behavior from routing or restoration problems. The dashboard intentionally does not display the raw upstream body or vault contents.

docs.title: 7. Switch to strict and see the difference
docs.text:
Edit only the profile in the tutorial YAML:

Partial edit inside the existing policy block
policy:
  profile: strict
  on_error: block
  unsupported: block

All tutorial rules omit action, so they inherit the new profile. Audit is already enabled with on_error: block. Validate the file in another terminal (substitute the tutorial path printed in step 1), then click Reload config.

The header should show profile: strict. Test the same string. The dashboard now reports error: blocked by policy (rule=…, class=…); no sanitized text is returned. A complete model request that matches any rule is refused before reaching the backend. Strict applies to inspected workspace metadata and protocol fields too, so a plain-looking prompt may still be blocked.

To mask ordinary values while blocking only selected categories, use the selective blocking recipe. Do not try to override strict with action: sanitize: validation rejects it.

docs.title: 8. Inspect a real request decision
docs.text:
Hover over a completed live-feed row to find its request ID. In a second terminal, replace the example placeholders with your tutorial config path and that ID:

cui-proxy explain -config /path/to/tutorial/config.yaml REQUEST-ID
cui-proxy audit verify -config /path/to/tutorial/config.yaml

String previews do not create decision records. Use a model request from step 6. The explanation records the decision, reason, and rule counts without the text or sensitive values. Hash-chain verification checks log integrity within its documented limits.

docs.title: 9. Finish the exercise
docs.text:
Exit the temporary Codex session, then stop the tutorial proxy with Ctrl-C in its terminal. Memory-vault mappings disappear at shutdown. The private tutorial directory remains for inspection; remove it when you no longer need the exercise.

You can now apply the same cycle to your normal YAML: add only the rules you need, validate, use fabricated positive and negative samples, reload, and verify the actual Codex route. See recipes for complete starting points and configuration for operational details.

docs.title: Manual verification against the real Codex CLI
Before reading demo materials in an assistant session
docs.text:
When the assistant itself connects through the proxy, reading a file is part of the next model request: tool output is sent back as conversation history. Keep configuration, /api/config, cloud CLI examples, fixture-runner source and detailed test reports local. Even a regex definition or a fabricated assignment can match an explicit blocking rule. A passing demo guide does not imply that the files it links to will pass.

Capture both output streams when running fixture checks. For example, this checks a local demo guide without returning its contents or replacement text:

python3 - <<'PYCODE'
from pathlib import Path
import re
import subprocess

config = Path.home() / ".config/cui-proxy/config.yaml"
guide = Path.home() / "cui-proxy-demo.md"
result = subprocess.run(
    ["cui-proxy", "test-rules", "-config", str(config)],
    input=guide.read_bytes(), capture_output=True,
)
rules = sorted(set(re.findall(rb"rule=([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)", result.stderr)))
print("Guide preview exit:", result.returncode)
print("Blocking rules:", ", ".join(r.decode() for r in rules) or "none reported")
if result.returncode and not rules:
    print("Preview failed; inspect the captured error locally.")
PYCODE

Apply the same capture discipline to fixture runners; report only status, rule names and counts. Do not print their source or full JSON reports to understand a failure. Run intentional block probes outside the assistant's conversation and inspect detailed results locally.

For a repeated HTTP 422 with reason=policy kind=rule_match, confirm the decision using cui-proxy explain and the request ID. Once triggering text is in history, start a fresh session with these precautions. Keep the active blocking policy; retrying the same history will not remove the trigger.

Status: live backend smoke passed on 2026-11-07. Built from this checkout on macOS arm64 with Go 1.26.10; exercised Codex CLI 0.167.0, ChatGPT login, model gpt-6-astra, and reasoning effort low. Only fabricated prompts were used, from an empty scratch directory, with command-line provider overrides; the global Codex configuration was unchanged.

docs.title: Recorded results
docs.text:
Recorded run summary contains versions, case outcomes, metrics, and scope without session credentials.

Check Observed result Live routing and authentication GET /v1/models and POST /v1/responses returned HTTP 200 Greeting Exact reply CUI_PROXY_LIVE_OK IP and OCID restoration Exact fabricated originals returned: 10.20.30.15 and the fabricated instance identifier Shell tool round trip Codex executed printf "host=10.20.30.15 done\n"; shell output and final reply contained the original fabricated IP Resent history The second tool-turn request recorded three IPv4 replacements, covering the restored history/tool output Decision log The baseline live-run chain passed audit verify; logs contained no fabricated prompt values

The baseline run recorded 8 requests, 6 replacements and 16 rewritten events. It reported zero errors, zero passthroughs, and zero audit-write failures. restores counts rewritten events, including buffered delta re-chunking; it is not the number of distinct restored values.

Live testing found that the Responses endpoint can omit Content-Type on its SSE response. Header-only classification skipped restoration. The proxy now probes an unlabelled, unencoded response on a sanitizing route and applies SSE restoration when its framing matches. Regression tests cover the missing header, comments, BOM, leading blank lines, and unchanged JSON error bodies.

This smoke covers text and a function tool call over HTTP/SSE. Long-session compaction, websocket transport, image input, and custom apply_patch events are outside this run's coverage. Existing content restrictions still apply.

docs.title: Workspace metadata smoke (2026-11-08)
docs.text:
The recorded metadata run used a synthetic Git repository with an SSH remote and the saved default routing, without provider overrides. The installed v0.3.1 returned HTTP 422 with reason header; the local v0.3.1+metadata.1 patch returned HTTP 200 and exact reply PROBE_OK 10.20.30.15 under the same eight-rule policy. Its temporary audit chain verified. This is evidence for workspace metadata and fabricated prompt restoration, not every possible request body or transport. The metadata fix is included in v0.3.2.

To repeat, use a scratch Git repository with a fabricated SSH remote such as git@github.com:example/demo.git, keep email detection enabled, and ask for an exact fabricated IP reply. Confirm successful restoration and metadata replacement counts. Strict or explicit block rules should still reject a matching remote. Never put real restricted values in a probe or its report.

docs.title: JSON escape dataflow regression (2026-11-08)
docs.text: The dataflow report covers the later reason=sanitize kind=bad_body failure after tool execution. The repair scans decoded JSON content, preserves structure, and restores function arguments using complete JSON tokens. Automated HTTP/SSE tests cover nested tool output, metadata, repeated sanitization and exact restoration; chunk-split tests compare streamed and completed arguments. An offline replay of the failing local tool output succeeds with the existing policy. This is separate from the live backend runs above; no live service was upgraded.

docs.title: Check the active policy before repeating a smoke
docs.text:
The results above describe dated, isolated runs, not the installed policy. On 2026-11-09 the local installation reported v0.5.0 and 13 configured rules, including five custom OCI rules with action: block. Those counts are a snapshot of that installation, not defaults or requirements. A sanitizing profile still honors explicit blocking rules. Updating a walkthrough cannot make an identifier restoration probe pass a rule that intentionally blocks it.

Check the installed version with cui-proxy version. Inspect live configuration locally in the dashboard; avoid copying the full /api/config response into an assistant session because patterns and dictionary entries can themselves match the active rules. Use the following offline check for a fabricated identifier. It generates the input locally, captures both CLI output streams, and prints only the outcome:

python3 - <<'PYCODE'
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess

config = Path.home() / ".config/cui-proxy/config.yaml"
identifier = ".".join(["ocid1", "instance", "oc1", "", "fabricated123"])
result = subprocess.run(
    ["cui-proxy", "test-rules", "-config", str(config)],
    input=identifier.encode(), capture_output=True,
)
if result.returncode == 0:
    print("Identifier probe: accepted; inspect replacement counts locally.")
elif b"blocked by policy" in result.stderr:
    print("Identifier probe: blocked by the configured policy (expected for block rules).")
else:
    raise SystemExit("Identifier probe failed; inspect the CLI error locally.")
PYCODE

Do not print the generated identifier, sanitized CLI output, or full fixtures back into a proxied assistant conversation. A synthetic value can still match a blocking rule. Once such text enters tool output or conversation history, later requests can repeat the same HTTP 422 because that history is resent. A fresh session avoids resending the old text; reading the same fixture into that session reintroduces it. Keep intentional block probes local and report only status, rule name and counts. Do not weaken blocking rules to run a demo.

docs.title: Repeat the isolated sanitizing smoke
docs.text: You run this by hand, once, on your own machine, with your own Codex login. Use only fabricated prompts, not pre-sanitized placeholders. Step 6 uses a fabricated IP; never substitute a real restricted value. This smoke uses a throwaway builtin-only policy, not the active custom blocking policy.

docs.title: 0. Before you start
docs.text:
• Codex CLI is installed and signed in with ChatGPT (codex login).
  • Your global ~/.codex/config.toml is never edited. The provider is passed with -c flags only, so nothing persists after this test.
  • Keep a second terminal free for the proxy's log.

docs.title: 1. Build
docs.text:
cd cui-proxy
make build                      # -> bin/cui-proxy
bin/cui-proxy version

docs.title: 2. Minimal config
docs.text:
Use a throwaway directory and unused ports (18787/18788 below) so the existing proxy and its policy stay active. Stop if either port is occupied:

mkdir -p /tmp/cui-verify && cd /tmp/cui-verify
cat > config.yaml <<'YAML'
listen: 127.0.0.1:18787
ui: { listen: 127.0.0.1:18788 }
upstreams:
  codex: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex
policy: { on_error: block }
vault: { mode: memory }
rules:
  - name: builtin
    type: builtin
YAML
/path/to/cui-proxy/bin/cui-proxy check-config -config config.yaml   # expect: ok: 1 rules

docs.title: 3. Start the proxy
docs.text:
/path/to/cui-proxy/bin/cui-proxy serve -config config.yaml

Expect startup lines like proxy listening on http://127.0.0.1:18787, dashboard on http://127.0.0.1:18788/ and upstream: https://chatgpt.com. Open http://127.0.0.1:18788/ in a browser.

docs.title: 4. Point a throwaway Codex run at the proxy
docs.text:
In a second terminal, from an empty scratch directory:

mkdir -p /tmp/cui-verify/work && cd /tmp/cui-verify/work
codex exec \
  -c 'model_provider="cui-proxy"' \
  -c 'model_providers.cui-proxy={name="cui-proxy",base_url="http://127.0.0.1:18787/v1",wire_api="responses",requires_openai_auth=true}' \
  "say hi" </dev/null

</dev/null matters: without it codex exec waits for stdin.

docs.title: 5. What to look for (first prompt)
docs.text:
On success, Codex prints a short greeting. Then check:

  • The dashboard's request feed has a POST /v1/responses with status 200 and no blocked reason. One or two GET /v1/models may appear before it (they are passed through).
  • The proxy log has no request blocked or upstream request failed line, and contains no token, account id, prompt text or URL query.
  • replacements stays near 0 for this prompt. The Codex system prompt can still match a rule; if so, the feed shows the rule names and counts only.

If something fails, check these in order:

Symptom Meaning / what to change Codex prints a 404 from the upstream, or the feed shows status 404 The path mapping is wrong. The proxy sends POST <upstream base> + /responses, i.e. https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses. Find the path Codex uses without the proxy (e.g. RUST_LOG=codex_core=debug codex exec "say hi" </dev/null against the default provider, and look for the request URL; debug logs can contain auth headers, so do not share them and delete them afterwards). Then change either upstreams.codex in the config (the base) or the route's UpstreamPath in internal/adapter/codex/codex.go (Match), and the "Point Codex at the proxy" section of configuration.md to match. GET /v1/models maps to <base>/models the same way. 401 / 403 from the upstream The auth headers did not arrive. Check that requires_openai_auth=true is in the -c flag. The proxy forwards Authorization and Chatgpt-Account-Id untouched. 422 policy / rule_match block A rule intentionally blocks matching content, including fabricated fixtures in tool output or resent history. Run intentional block checks locally with captured output; use a fresh session if history already contains the trigger. See the active-policy check above. 422 header block Codex workspaces and cwd metadata is sanitized using the active rules. Strict/block rules, malformed or oversized metadata, and detected values in unchanged metadata fields, other headers or queries still block. Inspect the reported kind and rule; do not disable email detection to allow SSH Git remotes. 422 sanitize / unrestorable block The body could not be sanitized. The error message and the log line name a kind and the rule, e.g. reason=sanitize kind=pool_exhausted rule=builtin.ipv4; see Block diagnostics. No value is ever printed. 403 route on an unexpected POST path, typically after a long session Codex called an endpoint the adapter does not know, most likely remote compaction (it advertises X-Codex-Beta-Features: remote_compaction_v2; the path may be e.g. /v1/responses/compact). The feed shows the path as (unmatched); find the real path with the debug log as in the 404 row. Add it as a KindSanitize route in Match in internal/adapter/codex/codex.go (its body is the same kind of history, so the request sanitizer applies). Note that a successful non-SSE response is refused until the adapter supports safe restoration for that format. 502 upstream_redirect The upstream answered with a 3xx. The proxy never relays redirects, so the base URL is probably wrong (see the 404 row). 502 stream_rewrite or a stream cut mid-answer An SSE event the rewriter could not handle. Note the event names from the open items below and report them.

docs.title: 6. Second prompt: made-up IP
docs.text:
codex exec \
  -c 'model_provider="cui-proxy"' \
  -c 'model_providers.cui-proxy={name="cui-proxy",base_url="http://127.0.0.1:18787/v1",wire_api="responses",requires_openai_auth=true}' \
  "Reply with exactly this text and nothing else: host 10.20.30.15" </dev/null

Expect:

  • The dashboard records at least one builtin.ipv4 replacement. vault_size grows by at least one mapping.
  • Codex's answer shows the original fabricated IP, 10.20.30.15. The model received a synthetic address and the proxy restored it. If the answer still contains a synthetic address, restoration missed an event type. Record which one (see coverage notes).
  • The proxy log shows no IP or OCID, only rule names and counts.

Optional tool-call check (the main restore path): ask "Run: echo 10.20.30.15" in a sandboxed run. The command Codex executes, and the function_call_output it sends back next turn, must show the original value locally, while the dashboard counts the value again on the second request (the resent history is sanitized again).

docs.title: 6a. Tool output with addresses (downgrade and addr.port)
docs.text:
In a sandboxed run, ask Codex to run a command whose output holds an IPv6 address, a label:fe80::1 form and tcpdump-style text (all made up):

codex exec \
  -c 'model_provider="cui-proxy"' \
  -c 'model_providers.cui-proxy={name="cui-proxy",base_url="http://127.0.0.1:18787/v1",wire_api="responses",requires_openai_auth=true}' \
  "Run: printf 'addr fd12:3456:789a::5 id:fe80::1\nIP 10.20.30.15.443 > 10.20.30.16.51234: Flags [S]\n' and then tell me which addresses appear" </dev/null

Expect:

  • No unrestorable or sanitize block in the feed or the log, on this request or on the following ones (the history with the tool output is resent every turn).
  • The Downgraded card counts at least 1 (id:fe80::1 is masked as a REDACTED-<8hex> token because an address synthetic glued to id: would not restore) and grows again on each later request of the same session.
  • The tcpdump endpoints are counted under builtin.secret (each addr.port token is masked whole); fd12:3456:789a::5 under builtin.ipv6.
  • Codex's answer and the local command output show the original values.

docs.title: 6b. Long session (remote compaction)
docs.text:
Run one interactive session (plain codex with the same -c flags) long enough for Codex to compact its context, for example by asking it to read and summarize several large files in the scratch directory. Watch the feed for any request other than POST /v1/responses and GET /v1/models:

  • A 403 route with path (unmatched) means a compaction (or other) endpoint is not routed; see the 403 row in the table above.
  • If compaction goes through POST /v1/responses, note it under the open items.

Stop the proxy with Ctrl-C. Memory mode discards every mapping.

docs.title: 6c. Decision log
docs.text:
With the proxy stopped (Ctrl-C), check that every request of the session was recorded and that the chain verifies. Use the same -config as serve:

/path/to/cui-proxy/bin/cui-proxy audit verify -config config.yaml   # expect: Result: OK, exit 0

Expect Records checked to be at least the number of requests in the feed, and the decision log (default ~/.local/state/cui-proxy/decisions.jsonl, mode 0600) to contain no IP, OCID, prompt text, header or path, only rule names and counts. Copy a request_id from a blocked request's error message (or from the X-Cui-Proxy-Request-Id header) and run cui-proxy explain -config config.yaml <id>: it should name the reason and the rule. Then make a copy of the log, delete one middle line from the copy and run cui-proxy audit verify -file <copy>: it must report the first break at that line and exit 1. See decision-log.md.

docs.title: 7. Record the result
docs.text:
Write down, for this repo:

  1. Whether https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex + /responses worked. If not, the base and path that did, plus the code/docs change made.
  2. Codex CLI version (codex --version).
  3. Answers to the open items below, including the compaction path (6b) and the X-Codex-Turn-Metadata shape.

docs.title: Coverage notes and follow-up checks
docs.text:
The live smoke established the core route and restoration path; broader sessions can exercise the additional cases below:

  • Confirmed routing: /v1/responses -> /backend-api/codex/responses and /v1/models -> /backend-api/codex/models returned HTTP 200 in the live smoke.
  • Trailing-delta fields: real delta events carry sequence_number and obfuscation. When the restorer re-chunks a held-back delta, it reuses the last delta event's fields. Codex accepted the text and function-tool streams in the live smoke; continue watching sequence handling in longer sessions.
  • Event names: reasoning-summary events (response.reasoning_summary_text.delta, response.reasoning_summary_part.done) and the custom-tool input event (response.custom_tool_call_input.delta, used by apply_patch). Any other *.delta event passes through unrestored, so a synthetic in it would reach the user as is.
  • Redirects: whether Codex follows redirects (the proxy turns every 3xx except 304 into a 502 anyway).
  • Header shapes: the exact names and contents of Session-Id, Thread-Id, X-Codex-Turn-Metadata and X-Codex-Beta-Features. These are inspected and can cause a header block; workspaces and cwd in turn metadata are sanitized. Additional client shapes need synthetic verification.
  • Additional transports and content: non-streaming, websocket, compaction and image requests are outside the recorded smoke coverage. Image parts are blocked by design. Remote compaction (remote_compaction_v2) probably uses its own endpoint, which today returns 403 route (step 6b); a route is added only once the real path is confirmed.
